mistakes: Using a hip swing to yank the sleeve instead of rowing with the back.
Letting the low back round as the arm reaches long.
Turning the lift into a biceps curl by leaving the shoulder blade stuck.
Standing too upright so the arc never loads the lats.
benefits: Rows one side at a time so left-to-right gaps show up immediately.
The fixed arc is easier on the low back than a free barbell row for some lifters.
Uses a standard barbell plus a sleeve, so it does not need a dedicated T-bar.

name: Barbell Lunge
summary: A loaded forward lunge with plates on the bar, stepping out, dropping, then returning the front foot to a standing start.
instructions: Unrack a loaded barbell across the upper traps and step into a clear space.
Stand tall with the feet together, chest up, and the trunk braced.
Step one foot forward in the direction your chest faces and plant it flat.
Bend both knees until the front thigh is nearly horizontal and the rear knee nears the floor.
Push through the front foot and step it back to the original standing position.
Reset and repeat on the other leg, keeping the bar still on the back.
mistakes: Initiating by stepping a leg behind the body, which turns it into a reverse lunge.
Letting the front knee collapse inward under the plates.
Leaning the torso over the front thigh instead of staying upright.
Rushing the return so the feet never rest together between reps.
benefits: Loads a forward lunge heavier than dumbbells without taxing the grip.
Trains single-leg strength while the bar forces an upright trunk.
Returns to a standing start, so it fits a shorter floor than a walking lunge.

name: Barbell Muscle Snatch
summary: A snatch variation that pulls the bar from the floor to overhead with no dip under — a strict-strength teaching lift for the snatch.
instructions: Stand with feet hip-width apart and the bar over mid-foot, gripping it wide with a flat back.
Pull the slack out of the bar, brace your core, and take a deep breath into your stomach.
Drive through the floor and pull the bar up the body, keeping it close as the hips extend.
Continue pulling the bar overhead in one smooth motion using the shoulders without dipping under.
Finish standing tall with the bar locked out overhead, biceps near the ears and core braced.
Lower the bar back to the front of the hips, then to the floor with control before the next rep.
mistakes: Bending the knees to dip under the bar, which turns the lift into a power snatch and loses the strict pull.
Pulling the bar away from the body, which forces the lower back to compensate at lockout.
Pressing the bar out at the top instead of pulling it overhead, which strains the shoulders.
Using too much weight, which breaks the strict pattern and removes the teaching benefit.
benefits: Builds strict pulling and pressing strength from floor to overhead.
Teaches the snatch path without the demand of a deep catch.
Strengthens the lower back, glutes, and shoulders as one chain.

name: Barbell Overhead Press
summary: The standing strict press from shoulders to overhead — the gold-standard test of pure shoulder strength and bracing.
instructions: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart and rack the bar across the front of the shoulders just under the chin.
Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder width with the wrists stacked over the elbows.
Brace your core, squeeze the glutes, and take a big breath to lock the torso in place.
Press the bar straight up by pushing through the shoulders and triceps, moving your head back slightly.
Lock out the arms overhead with the bar over the middle of the foot and biceps near the ears.
Lower the bar back to the front of the shoulders under control, reset your breath, and repeat.
mistakes: Pressing the bar in front of the head instead of straight up, which strains the lower back and shoulders.
Leaning back excessively to turn the lift into an incline press, which overloads the spine.
Failing to brace the core, which lets the rib cage flare and weakens the press.
Bending the knees and using leg drive, which makes the lift a push press and not a strict press.
benefits: Builds strict overhead pressing strength in the shoulders and triceps.
Develops core bracing and full-body stability under load.
Adds shoulder size for a wider, more capped upper body.

name: Barbell Power Snatch
summary: An explosive pull from the floor to overhead, caught in a quarter squat — full-body power without the depth of a full snatch.
instructions: Stand with feet hip-width apart and the bar over mid-foot, gripping the bar wide with a flat back.
Pull the slack out of the bar, brace your core, and take a deep breath into your belly.
Drive the legs into the floor and accelerate the bar up the body as the hips extend explosively.
Pull yourself under the bar quickly and catch it overhead with arms locked out and elbows tight.
Stop the catch in a quarter-squat position with the bar stable directly over the middle of the foot.
Stand fully tall, then lower the bar back to the hips and down to the floor under control.
mistakes: Pulling with the arms early instead of driving the legs and hips first, which kills bar speed.
Catching the bar with bent or soft elbows, which collapses the lockout and risks shoulder strain.
Letting the bar swing away from the body, which forces the lower back to recover the lift.
Catching too low into a full squat, which turns the power snatch into a regular snatch.
benefits: Builds explosive total-body power from floor to overhead.
Trains hip extension speed that carries over to sprints and jumps.
Develops overhead stability and quick under-the-bar mechanics.

name: Barbell Pullover
summary: A bench-based overhead arc that stretches and loads the lats — an old-school accessory for back, chest, and rib-cage development.
instructions: Lie back on a flat bench with your head supported and feet planted flat on the floor.
Hold a barbell over your chest with a shoulder-width grip and a slight bend in the elbows.
Brace your core and pull your shoulder blades back and down into the bench.
Lower the bar slowly in an arc behind your head until you feel a deep stretch in the lats.
Pause briefly at the bottom, keeping the elbow angle locked, then pull the bar back over the chest.
Stop the bar above the chest line and reset before the next controlled rep.
mistakes: Bending and straightening the elbows mid-rep, which turns the lift into a triceps extension.
Lowering the bar too fast, which strains the front shoulders without loading the lats.
Lifting the lower back off the bench, which removes tension from the lats and stresses the spine.
Using too much weight, which forces the elbows to collapse and breaks the overhead arc.
benefits: Builds lats through a deep loaded stretch most pulls miss.
Adds chest and serratus involvement as a secondary benefit.
Reinforces overhead shoulder mobility under controlled load.

name: Barbell Rack Pull
summary: A partial deadlift pulled from a raised pin position — heavy back loading without the demand of a full lift from the floor.
instructions: Set the safety pins in a rack at about knee height and load the bar to your working weight.
Stand with feet hip-width apart, bar over mid-foot, and grip just outside the knees.
Pull the slack out of the bar, brace the core, and pull the chest up tall with a flat back.
Drive the floor away with your legs while keeping the bar dragging close to your thighs.
Stand fully tall by squeezing the glutes and locking out the hips and knees together.
Lower the bar back to the pins under control, reset your breath, and repeat for clean reps.
mistakes: Setting the pins too low or too high, which removes the partial-lift benefit and risks form breakdown.
Rounding the upper back hard to grind the rep, which strains the spine under heavy load.
Hyperextending at the top instead of finishing with a tight glute squeeze and stacked rib cage.
Bouncing the bar off the pins and using momentum instead of resetting between reps.
benefits: Builds upper-back and trap thickness with heavier loads than full deadlifts.
Strengthens the deadlift lockout for stronger pulls overall.
Teaches the hinge pattern through a shorter, easier range.

name: Barbell Rear Delt Row
summary: A hinged wide-grip row that pulls the bar to the upper chest with the elbows flared, targeting the rear delts.
instructions: Grip a barbell with a wide overhand grip, well outside the shoulders.
Hinge at the hips until the torso is near parallel, with a soft knee bend and a flat back.
Let the bar hang at arm's length below the chest, elbows straight.
Pull the bar toward the upper chest with the elbows flared out to the sides.
Stop when the upper arms are roughly in line with the shoulders.
Lower the bar under control to a straight-arm hang and repeat.
mistakes: Tucking the elbows to the ribs, which turns the lift into a lat row.
Swinging the torso to yank the bar up.
Pulling the bar to the belly instead of high on the chest.
Using a load so heavy that the elbows never reach shoulder height.
benefits: Loads the rear delts with a barbell instead of only light dumbbell flies.
Trains the upper traps and rhomboids on the same horizontal-abduction path.
Gives a clear coaching contrast with a tucked-elbow bent-over row.

name: Barbell Reverse Lunge
summary: A lunge stepped backward with a barbell on the traps, loading the front leg while the rear leg guides balance.
instructions: Unrack a barbell across your traps and step back into a clear space.
Stand with your feet about shoulder width apart and brace your abdominals.
Step one foot straight backward while both knees begin to bend.
Lower until the rear knee is just above the floor and both knees sit near 90 degrees.
Push through the front foot to drive back to the standing position.
Reset your stance and repeat on the other leg.
mistakes: Leaning the torso back to stand up, which hyperextends the spine under the bar.
Taking too short a step, which crowds the front knee forward over the toes.
Letting the front knee drift inward as you drive up, which stresses the joint.
Landing the rear foot off line, which narrows the base and costs balance under load.
benefits: Loads one leg at a time without the knee stress of a forward step.
Lets you bias the quads or the glutes by changing step length.
Builds balance and left to right symmetry under a real barbell load.

name: Barbell Romanian Deadlift
summary: A hip hinge that lowers a barbell along the thighs with the knees barely bent, loading the hamstrings.
instructions: Set the bar over your shoelaces and take a hip width stance.
Grip the bar just outside your hips and stand tall with the hips and knees locked.
Lift your chest, set your shoulder blades back and brace your abdominals.
Push your tailbone backward and lower the bar down the front of your legs.
Stop where your hamstrings stop stretching, keeping only a slight knee bend.
Press your feet into the floor and drive your hips forward to stand tall.
mistakes: Rounding the lower back instead of hinging at the hips, which loads the lumbar spine.
Bending the knees too much, which turns the lift into a squat and unloads the hamstrings.
Letting the bar drift away from the legs, which lengthens the lever on the lower back.
Looking up into a mirror, which extends the neck under load.
benefits: Loads the hamstrings through a long eccentric stretch under control.
Teaches the hip hinge pattern that every deadlift variation depends on.
Builds posterior chain strength without pulling from the floor.

name: Barbell Shrug
summary: A standing two-handed shrug that loads the upper traps — the classic move for trap thickness and a stronger neck-to-shoulder line.
instructions: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart and grip the barbell at the hips with hands shoulder-width apart.
Pull your shoulders down and back to start in a neutral position with arms fully extended.
Brace your core and keep the chest up so the torso stays still through the lift.
Shrug your shoulders straight up toward your ears as high as you can without bending the elbows.
Pause for a second at the top, squeezing the upper traps hard.
Lower the bar slowly back to the start over 2 to 3 seconds, keeping tension on the traps.
mistakes: Rolling the shoulders forward and back instead of shrugging straight up, which strains the joints.
Bending the elbows to help cheat the bar up, which turns the move into a partial upright row.
Using too much weight and cutting the range short with tiny shrugs that miss the contraction.
Letting the chin jut forward, which loads the neck instead of the upper traps.
benefits: Builds upper-trap size for a thicker neck-to-shoulder line.
Strengthens the shrug pattern that supports heavy carries and deadlifts.
Strengthens the grip as a side benefit of holding heavy loads.

name: Barbell Skullcrusher
summary: A lying elbow-extension lift on a flat bench, lowering a barbell toward the forehead then pressing it back to lockout.
instructions: Lie on a flat bench with both feet on the floor and a barbell held over the shoulders.
Grip the bar overhand at about shoulder width, palms facing away.
Lock the upper arms vertical so the elbows point toward the ceiling.
Bend only the elbows and lower the bar in an arc to about an inch from the forehead.
Extend the elbows and return the bar over the shoulders without locking out hard.
Keep the head, back, and hips on the bench for every rep.
mistakes: Flaring the elbows out so the shoulders and chest take over.
Lowering the upper arms toward the chest, which turns the lift into a press.
Bouncing the bar off the forehead instead of stopping short.
Locking the elbows hard at the top and dumping tension off the triceps.
benefits: Isolates elbow extension with a barbell that is easy to load.
Keeps the upper arms still so the triceps, not the chest, do the work.
Pairs with pressing days as a direct arm accessory.

name: Barbell Snatch
summary: The full Olympic snatch — bar from the floor to overhead in one pull, caught in a deep overhead squat.
instructions: Stand with feet hip-width apart and the bar over mid-foot, gripping the bar wide with a flat back.
Pull the slack out of the bar, brace the core, and take a deep breath into the belly.
Drive through the floor and accelerate the bar up the body as the hips extend explosively.
Pull yourself under the bar fast and catch it overhead with arms locked out in a deep overhead squat.
Stand up out of the squat with the bar held tight overhead and the core fully braced.
Lower the bar to the front of the hips and down to the floor under control before the next rep.
mistakes: Yanking the bar with the arms early instead of letting the legs and hips drive the pull.
Catching the bar with soft elbows, which collapses the lockout and risks shoulder injury.
Letting the bar drift forward, which forces a missed lift or a heavy lower-back save.
Skipping the squat depth and catching too high, which turns the snatch into a power snatch.
benefits: Builds explosive power across the back, glutes, and hamstrings.
Trains overhead mobility and stability under maximum speed.
Develops timing and coordination that no other lift teaches.

name: Barbell Spinal Jefferson Curl
summary: A slow loaded spinal flexion with a light barbell — a controlled mobility drill that strengthens the back through full forward bending.
instructions: Stand on a low box holding a light barbell at the front of your hips with arms extended.
Tuck your chin to your chest and slowly start rolling the spine downward one segment at a time.
Continue rolling forward through the upper back, then the mid-back, then the lower back.
Allow the bar to drift down toward the feet, keeping the legs straight and the bar close to the body.
Pause briefly at the bottom in a deep forward fold with the spine fully rounded.
Reverse the motion by stacking up segment by segment from the lower back back to the head.
mistakes: Using too heavy a load, which forces the back to grind instead of moving slowly through each segment.
Bending at the hips like a stiff-leg deadlift instead of rolling through the spine.
Rushing the rep, which removes the controlled tissue loading that makes the drill useful.
Bending the knees to chase depth, which removes the hamstring stretch that pairs with the spinal work.
benefits: Builds tissue tolerance through full loaded spinal flexion.
Improves hamstring and back-of-body flexibility under control.
Trains segmental spinal control that carries over to lifting and movement.

name: Barbell Split Squat
summary: A loaded split-stance squat for single-leg quad and glute strength — the staircase between regular squats and Bulgarian split squats.
instructions: Rack the bar across the upper back and step into a long split stance with feet hip-width apart.
Brace your core and stand tall with most of your weight on the front foot.
Lower the back knee straight down toward the floor, keeping the front shin close to vertical.
Stop just before the back knee touches the floor, keeping the torso upright and chest up.
Drive through the front foot to stand back up to the starting split-stance position.
Complete all reps on one side before switching legs, keeping the same setup each time.
mistakes: Letting the front knee cave inward, which strains the knee and reduces glute engagement.
Pushing off the back foot to stand up, which removes load from the front working leg.
Leaning the torso too far forward, which turns the lift into a hinge and loses the quad focus.
Setting the stance too short, which forces the front knee far past the toes and stresses the joint.
benefits: Builds single-leg quad and glute strength with full barbell loading.
Exposes and corrects strength imbalances between legs.
Reinforces balance and core stability under a back-loaded bar.

name: Barbell Squat
summary: The back-loaded barbell squat — the king of lower-body strength training and the standard for measuring leg power.
instructions: Set the bar in a rack at about chest height and step under it to rack it across your upper back.
Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder width, brace your core, and step back from the rack.
Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, toes turned slightly out, and chest tall.
Push your hips back and down, bending the knees to squat down until your hips reach below the knees.
Drive through the full foot to stand back up, keeping the chest tall and bar path straight.
Lock out the hips and knees at the top, reset your breath and brace, and repeat for clean reps.
mistakes: Letting the knees cave inward on the way up, which strains the knees and weakens the drive.
Cutting the depth short and not reaching at least parallel, missing the full quad and glute work.
Rounding the lower back at the bottom, which puts the spine at risk under heavy load.
Shifting the bar weight onto the toes, which throws off the balance and strains the lower back.
benefits: Builds total lower-body strength led by the quads and glutes.
Trains core bracing and full-body stability under heavy load.
Reinforces the squat pattern that carries over to sport and daily life.

name: Barbell Step Up Knee Drive
summary: A back-racked step-up with a driving knee at the top — single-leg quad and glute strength with explosive hip drive built in.
instructions: Set a sturdy box at about knee height and rack the bar across your upper back.
Stand close to the box, brace your core, and place one foot fully flat on top of it.
Drive through the full foot on the box to stand tall, keeping the chest up and bar steady.
At the top, drive the trailing knee up and forward to hip height in a sprint-style action.
Lower that leg back down and step the foot off the box under control with no thud.
Reset to the starting position and repeat for the prescribed reps before switching legs.
mistakes: Pushing off the trailing leg instead of driving through the working leg on top of the box.
Choosing a box that's too tall, which forces a hip-shift and removes tension from the quads.
Letting the torso fold forward under the bar, which turns the lift into a heavy good morning.
Stepping down hard from the box, which beats up the joints and breaks position between reps.
benefits: Builds single-leg strength in the quads and glutes under a real load.
Trains explosive hip drive and knee lift for sprinting and jumping.
Improves balance and core control under a back-racked bar.

name: Barbell Stiff Leg Deadlifts
summary: A near-straight-legged hinge from the floor that loads the hamstrings and glutes through a deep stretch — a clean back-of-body builder.
instructions: Stand with feet hip-width apart and grip the bar just outside the knees with arms extended.
Stand tall holding the bar at the hips, then unlock the knees with a small soft bend.
Push the hips back and lower the bar down the legs by hinging at the hips, keeping the back flat.
Continue lowering until you feel a strong stretch in the hamstrings, with the bar staying close to the legs.
Drive the hips forward and squeeze the glutes hard to stand back up to the starting position.
Lock out the hips at the top with a tall chest, reset your breath, and repeat for clean reps.
mistakes: Locking the knees fully straight, which turns the lift into a back-stress machine instead of a hamstring builder.
Rounding the lower back at the bottom, which loads the spine instead of stretching the hamstrings.
Letting the bar drift away from the legs, which crushes the lower back at the bottom range.
Bending the knees too much, which turns the lift back into a regular deadlift.
benefits: Builds hamstring size and strength through a deep loaded stretch.
Develops glute strength at the lockout for full hip-drive power.
Reinforces clean hinge mechanics that carry over to deadlifts.

name: Barbell Thruster
summary: A front squat into an overhead press in one motion — the conditioning workhorse that hits legs, shoulders, and lungs at once.
instructions: Set the bar in a front-rack position across the front of your shoulders with elbows lifted high.
Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, brace your core, and keep your chest tall throughout the lift.
Drop into a full front squat by sitting your hips back and tracking your knees over your toes.
Drive hard out of the bottom and use that leg drive to launch the bar off your shoulders.
Press the bar overhead in one fluid motion, finishing with arms locked out and biceps near your ears.
Lower the bar back to the front rack under control and reset for the next rep without pausing.
mistakes: Pressing the bar with arms only instead of using the leg drive out of the squat to power the press.
Dropping the elbows in the front rack, which collapses the chest and dumps the bar forward.
Cutting the squat depth short to save energy, turning the lift into a half-rep push press.
Catching the bar on the shoulders too hard on the way down, which beats up the front delts over volume.
benefits: Builds full-body strength and conditioning in a single compound movement.
Trains leg drive into overhead pressing for athletic power transfer.
Spikes heart rate fast, making it a high-return conditioning lift.

name: Barbell Upright Row
summary: A vertical pull from the hips to the chest that loads the side delts and traps — the classic shoulder-width builder.
instructions: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart and grip the bar with hands slightly narrower than shoulder width.
Let the bar hang at arm's length against your thighs with shoulders pulled back and chest up.
Pull the bar straight up by leading with the elbows, keeping the bar close to your body the whole way.
Stop the pull when your upper arms are roughly parallel to the floor — do not crank the elbows higher.
Pause briefly at the top and feel the side delts and upper traps working under the load.
Lower the bar back down under control over 2 to 3 seconds, then reset for the next rep.
mistakes: Pulling the bar too high past shoulder level, which jams the shoulder joint and risks front-shoulder strain.
Using a grip that is too narrow, which forces the wrists into an awkward angle and shifts work off the delts.
Heaving the bar up with body english instead of leading with the elbows in a controlled pull.
Letting the bar drift away from the body, which kills side-delt tension and loads the lower back.
benefits: Builds the side delts and upper traps for a wider shoulder shape.
Trains the vertical pull pattern as a complement to overhead pressing.
Develops shoulder and trap thickness for a stronger upper-body silhouette.

name: Barbell Walking Lunge
summary: A traveling forward lunge with a barbell on the traps, stepping through each rep instead of returning to a standing start.
instructions: Unrack a barbell across the upper traps and walk into a clear lane.
Stand tall with the feet about hip-width apart and brace the trunk.
Step one foot forward and bend both knees as you drop.
Lower until the rear knee is just above the floor and both knees are near 90 degrees.
Drive through the front foot, stand, and step the rear leg through into the next lunge.
Keep alternating down the lane without pausing in a feet-together stance.
mistakes: Returning the rear foot to a standing start instead of walking through.
Letting the front knee cave in as you step.
Leaning the torso forward under the bar.
Taking such a long stride that you cannot control the drop.
benefits: Loads a gait-like lunge that an in-place lunge does not.
Builds single-leg strength and trunk stiffness under a moving bar.
Lets programs prescribe distance or steps instead of only pairs of reps.

name: Barbell Wrist Curl
summary: A small-range wrist flexion that isolates the forearm flexors — the classic finisher for grip strength and forearm size.
instructions: Sit on a bench and rest your forearms on your thighs with your wrists hanging just past the knees.
Hold the bar with an underhand grip, hands shoulder-width apart, and let it roll into your fingertips.
Curl the bar up by closing your fingers and flexing your wrists, keeping the forearms pinned to your thighs.
Squeeze hard at the top with the wrists fully flexed and feel the forearms contract.
Lower the bar back down under control, letting it roll out toward the fingertips at the bottom.
Repeat for high reps, focusing on a slow tempo and a full range from fingertips to top squeeze.
mistakes: Lifting the forearms off the thighs, which lets the biceps take over instead of isolating the forearms.
Using too much weight and shortening the range so the bar barely moves at the wrist.
Skipping the fingertip roll at the bottom, which cuts out half the forearm and grip work.
Rushing the tempo and bouncing the reps, which removes the time-under-tension that builds the forearms.
benefits: Builds forearm size and grip strength through direct isolation.
Strengthens wrist flexion for sport, lifting, and climbing.
Improves grip endurance for heavier pulling and carrying work.

name: Battle Ropes
summary: Anchored rope waves driven from an athletic stance, holding vigorous intensity while arms, trunk and hips all work.
instructions: Anchor the rope at its midpoint and take one end in each hand.
Stand facing the anchor with feet hip to shoulder width and knees softly bent.
Hinge slightly at the hips, brace your trunk and let your arms hang ready.
Drive both hands up and down together to send continuous waves down the rope.
Keep the wave alive for the full work interval instead of pausing between reps.
Set the rope down and recover actively before the next interval starts.
mistakes: Standing upright with locked knees, which cuts the hips out and strands the work in the arms.
Letting the wave die mid-interval, so intensity drops well below the target range.
Gripping so tightly that the forearms fail before the trunk and shoulders are trained.
Rounding the lower back on slams, which loads the spine instead of the trunk musculature.
benefits: Reaches vigorous cardiorespiratory intensity without running or jumping.
Recruits shoulders, trunk, hips and grip in one continuous pattern.
Scales by rope thickness, length and interval length rather than added load.

name: Bayesian Curl
summary: Single arm cable curl performed with the elbow held behind the torso so the biceps stay loaded in the stretch.
instructions: Set a single handle on the lowest pulley and select a light weight.
Face away from the stack and take the handle with your palm forward.
Step forward until the cable is taut and your working elbow sits behind your ribs.
Brace your abs and lean slightly forward in a split stance.
Bend the elbow to curl the handle toward your shoulder without letting the elbow move forward.
Lower under control back into the stretch, finish the set, then swap arms.
mistakes: Not stepping far enough from the stack, so the arm never gets behind the body and the stretch is lost.
Letting the elbow drift forward, which turns the lift into an ordinary cable curl.
Loading too heavy, so the shoulder and torso swing the handle up instead of the biceps.
Standing square to the cable, which drags the wire across the wrist and cuts the range short.
benefits: Holds the biceps under load at a long muscle length where free weight curls go slack.
Constant cable tension across the whole range, including the bottom of the rep.
Unilateral loading exposes and evens out side to side differences.

name: Bear Crawl
summary: A quadruped crawl with the knees hovering just off the floor, travelling by stepping opposite hand and opposite foot together.
instructions: Start on all fours with the wrists under the shoulders and the knees under the hips.
Tuck the toes, brace the trunk, and lift both knees one to two inches off the floor.
Keep the back flat and the hips level with the shoulders.
Step the right hand and left foot forward together a short, even distance.
Step the left hand and right foot forward next, keeping the knees hovering.
Continue the contralateral crawl for the desired distance or time, then reverse.
mistakes: Letting the hips pike up, which unloads the trunk and shoulders.
Sagging the lower back instead of holding a braced, nearly level spine.
Taking steps so large that the hips rock side to side.
Allowing the knees to tap the floor, which turns the crawl into a kneel shuffle.
benefits: Trains core control, shoulder stability, and hip coordination in one bodyweight pattern.
Raises the heart rate without impact, so it fits low-impact conditioning blocks.
Needs no equipment and only a short strip of floor, so it works in app and home programming.

name: Behind-the-Neck Press
summary: An overhead barbell press with the bar racked behind the neck, demanding full shoulder and thoracic mobility.
instructions: Set a barbell in a rack just below shoulder height and load a conservative weight.
Step under the bar and rest it across your upper traps with a grip wider than shoulder width.
Stand tall, brace your abdominals and glutes, then take two steps back from the rack.
Press the bar straight overhead, keeping the torso upright and the chin tucked.
Lock out with the bar over the middle of your head and your ears close to your arms.
Lower the bar under control back onto the upper traps and repeat only while form holds.
mistakes: Attempting the lift without full overhead mobility, which forces the head forward and strains the shoulder.
Dropping the bar quickly onto the traps, which risks contact with the neck and head.
Using leg drive, which turns a strict press into a push press and hides a load that is too heavy.
Leaning back to finish the rep, which shifts the load onto the lower back.
benefits: Keeps the bar path vertical, which places steady demand on the lateral deltoid.
Exposes shoulder and thoracic mobility limits that front pressing can mask.
Builds overhead stability for lifters who already press comfortably from the front.

name: Belt Squat
summary: A squat loaded through a hip belt on a machine, so the weight pulls at the hips instead of sitting on the spine.
instructions: Fasten the hip belt around your pelvis and attach it to the machine.
Stand on the platform so the attachment point sits directly between your feet.
Set your feet at about shoulder width with the toes turned out slightly.
Take the weight, release the safeties and hold the frame lightly for balance.
Drop your hips straight down until your thighs reach roughly parallel.
Drive through your whole foot to stand tall and repeat.
mistakes: Standing off center so the cable pulls to one side, which twists the hips.
Pulling on the frame with the arms, which quietly removes load from the legs.
Loading it like a leg press, which overwhelms the belt position and cuts the range short.
Letting the hips travel backward instead of straight down, which turns it into a hinge.
benefits: Loads the legs hard while keeping low back moments lower than a back squat.
Removes the shoulder and wrist mobility demand of racking a bar.
Lets lifters keep squatting when spinal loading has to be limited.

name: Bench Dips
summary: A bodyweight triceps dip off a bench or chair that builds arm pushing strength — the go-to home and hotel-room arm exercise.
instructions: Sit on the edge of a sturdy bench or chair and grip the edge with hands just outside your hips.
Slide your hips off the bench and walk your feet out so your weight is supported by your arms.
Lower your body slowly by bending your elbows straight back until your upper arms are roughly parallel to the floor.
Keep your back close to the bench and your shoulders pulled down away from your ears the whole way.
Pause briefly at the bottom with the triceps loaded, then press through your palms back up to the start.
Lock out the arms at the top without shrugging the shoulders, then repeat for the prescribed reps.
mistakes: Letting the elbows flare out to the sides, which loads the front shoulders instead of the triceps.
Letting the shoulders shrug up toward the ears, which strains the front shoulders under the dip.
Cutting the depth short to make the reps easier, which removes most of the triceps work.
Using only the legs to push off the floor, which turns the dip into an assisted leg-press motion.
benefits: Builds triceps strength and size with no equipment needed.
Trains the pushing pattern in any home or travel setting.
Strengthens arm lockout for pressing and dipping movements.

name: Bent Over One-Arm Long Bar Row
summary: A hinged one-arm row of a barbell anchored at the far end, pulling the loaded sleeve toward the hip.
instructions: Wedge one end of a barbell into a corner or landmine sleeve and load the free end.
Stand over the bar with one foot on each side, knees soft, and hinge at the hips.
Grip the bar close to the plates with one hand and brace the other hand on the thigh.
Row the bar up by driving the elbow back and squeezing the shoulder blade.
Pause at the top, then lower until the arm is long without rounding the back.
Finish the set, then switch hands and match the same range.
mistakes: Rounding the low back as the arm reaches long.
Yanking the sleeve with a hip swing instead of rowing with the back.
Looking down so far that the spine flexes.
Turning the lift into a biceps curl by leaving the shoulder blade stuck.
benefits: Rows one side at a time so left-to-right gaps show up immediately.
The fixed arc is easier to steer than a free barbell row for some lifters.
Uses a standard barbell plus a corner, so it does not need a T-bar station.

name: Bent Over Two-Dumbbell Row Palms In
summary: A standing hip-hinge row with a dumbbell in each hand and palms facing in, loading the upper back and lats.
instructions: Stand with a dumbbell in each hand using a neutral grip, palms facing in.
Hinge at the hips with a slight knee bend until the torso sits just above horizontal.
Let the dumbbells hang below the shoulders with a flat back and braced abs.
Pull both elbows back and up until the weights reach the sides of the waist.
Squeeze the shoulder blades together at the top without shrugging the neck.
Lower the dumbbells under control to full arm extension and repeat.
mistakes: Rounding the lower back in the hinge, which loads the spine instead of the upper back.
Standing too upright, which turns the row into a shrug.
Jerking the torso up with each rep so momentum, not the back, moves the weights.
Flaring the elbows wide instead of keeping them close to the sides.
benefits: A neutral grip is easier on the wrists and shoulders than a palms-down row.
Two independent dumbbells stop one side from hiding a weaker pull.
Builds a hinge-and-row pattern that carries into heavier barbell rows.

name: Bent-Knee Soleus Raise
summary: A standing heel raise done with a constant knee bend on a low platform, biasing plantarflexion toward the soleus.
instructions: Stand on a low platform with the balls of both feet on the front edge and the heels free to hang.
Bend both knees slightly and hold that angle; do not squat deeper during the set.
Brace the trunk, keep the hips still, and clasp the hands behind the lower back or let them hang.
Lower both heels behind the platform until they approach the floor.
Press through the balls of the feet and raise the heels as high as the ankles allow.
Pause briefly at the top, then lower under control and repeat without changing the knee bend.
mistakes: Straightening the knees on the way up, which hands the work back to the gastrocnemius.
Bouncing out of the bottom instead of pausing in the stretched heel-drop.
Letting the hips rise and fall, which turns the raise into a mini squat.
Stopping the heels halfway down so the soleus never sees a full stretch.
benefits: Biases plantarflexion toward the soleus by keeping the knees bent.
Uses a small platform instead of a seated calf machine, so it fits bodyweight libraries.
Trains full heel travel, including a deficit stretch at the bottom.

name: Bicycle Crunches
summary: A floor core drill that starts in tabletop and cycles opposite elbow to opposite knee while one leg extends.
instructions: Lie face up with both hands behind the head and both hips and knees bent to about 90 degrees.
Keep the lower back on the floor and lift the head and upper shoulders only slightly.
Brace the abdominals so the tabletop position stays still before the first twist.
Rotate the trunk and draw one knee in as the opposite elbow comes toward that knee.
Extend the other leg long, then switch sides in a smooth pedal.
Return to tabletop between sides if needed, and do not pull the neck with the hands.
mistakes: Yanking the head with the hands instead of curling from the ribcage.
Letting the hips twist with the shoulders, which leaks the rotation out of the trunk.
Straightening both legs at once so the tabletop brace is lost.
Resting the head down between reps instead of keeping the shoulder blades slightly lifted.
benefits: Combines trunk flexion and rotation so rectus and obliques work in one cycle.
Starts from a clear tabletop position that is easy to show in a looping 3D clip.
Requires no kit, so it slots into home core circuits and app bodyweight collections.

name: Bird Dog
summary: A quadruped core drill that extends one arm and the opposite leg while the trunk resists rotation and extension.
instructions: Kneel on a mat and set each hand below its shoulder and each knee below its hip.
Brace your abdominals and set your spine flat with your neck in line with your back.
Extend one leg straight behind you until it is roughly parallel to the floor.
At the same time reach the opposite arm forward to shoulder height, keeping the hips level.
Hold briefly while resisting any rotation through the pelvis.
Return the hand and knee to the floor under control, then repeat on the other side.
mistakes: Letting the hips rotate toward the lifted leg, which removes the anti-rotation demand entirely.
Lifting the leg above hip height, which arches the lower back instead of loading the core.
Letting the chest sag between the shoulder blades, which shifts support onto the shoulder joints.
Rushing the reps, which replaces core control with momentum and balance corrections.
benefits: Trains the trunk to stay stable while the arms and legs move independently.
Requires no equipment and no floor space beyond a mat, so it suits home programming.
Loads the spine lightly, which makes it usable early in low back conditioning.

name: Bodyweight Alternating Lateral Lunge
summary: A side-to-side lunge that loads one leg at a time — builds glute and quad strength while opening up the inner thighs and hips.
instructions: Stand tall with feet together, hands at your chest, and your core braced for balance.
Take a wide step out to one side and plant the foot flat with toes pointing forward.
Sit your hips back and bend the stepping leg, keeping the trailing leg straight and the chest tall.
Lower until the working thigh is roughly parallel to the floor and you feel a stretch in the inner thigh.
Push through the heel of the working leg to drive back up to standing in one strong motion.
Repeat on the opposite side and continue alternating for the prescribed reps.
mistakes: Letting the knee of the working leg cave inward instead of tracking over the foot.
Leaning the chest too far forward, which loads the lower back instead of the glutes and quads.
Rounding the back when sitting into the lunge instead of hinging cleanly at the hips.
Cutting the depth short and turning a real lateral lunge into a shallow side step.
benefits: Builds glute and quad strength through a side-to-side hip pattern.
Opens up the inner thighs and improves lateral hip mobility.
Trains balance and single-leg control without weights.

name: Bodyweight Alternating Reverse Lunges
summary: A backward-stepping lunge that builds the glutes and quads — the knee-friendly cousin of the forward lunge.
instructions: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, hands on your hips or at your chest for balance.
Take a long step back with one leg and lower the back knee straight down toward the floor.
Drop until the back knee is just above the ground and the front thigh is roughly parallel to the floor.
Keep the front knee tracking over the front foot and your chest tall the entire descent.
Drive through the heel of the front foot to push yourself back up to standing in one strong motion.
Step back with the opposite leg and continue alternating for the prescribed reps.
mistakes: Taking too short a step back, which loads the front knee instead of the front glute.
Slamming the back knee into the floor instead of lowering it under control.
Letting the chest collapse forward, which shifts the work to the lower back.
Pushing off the back foot instead of driving through the front heel — robs the front leg of work.
benefits: Builds the glutes, quads, and hamstrings through a knee-friendly lunge pattern.
Trains single-leg balance and split-stance control.
Strengthens the lower body anywhere with no equipment needed.

name: Bodyweight Box Squat
summary: A bodyweight squat to a bench or box — the cleanest way to teach squat depth and hip-back mechanics to beginners.
instructions: Set a sturdy bench or box behind you and stand in front of it with feet shoulder-width apart.
Cross your arms in front of your chest or hold them straight out for balance.
Sit your hips back as if reaching for the box, keeping your chest tall and your weight in your heels.
Lower under control until your glutes touch the box softly — do not crash down onto it.
Pause briefly on the box without losing core or leg tension, staying ready to drive back up.
Push through the floor with both feet to stand back up tall, squeezing your glutes at the top.
mistakes: Plopping down onto the box instead of touching it under control, which kills the leg tension.
Squatting straight down instead of sitting the hips back, which loads the knees over the glutes.
Letting the knees cave inward as you stand back up, which weakens the lift and stresses the knees.
Rounding the lower back at the bottom — turns a teaching tool into a back-strain risk.
benefits: Teaches consistent squat depth without guesswork.
Builds quad and glute strength with controlled mechanics.
Improves squat confidence for new lifters before adding load.

name: Bodyweight Deadlift
summary: An unloaded hip hinge that teaches the deadlift pattern — the safest way to learn how to bend, brace, and stand back up.
instructions: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, arms hanging loose at your sides, and your core lightly braced.
Push your hips back as if closing a car door with your butt, letting your knees bend just slightly.
Hinge forward at the hips with a flat back and let your hands slide down the front of your thighs.
Lower until you feel a strong stretch in your hamstrings and your torso is roughly parallel to the floor.
Drive through your heels and squeeze your glutes hard to stand back up to a tall position.
Lock out at the top by squeezing the glutes — do not lean back, just stand fully upright.
mistakes: Squatting down instead of hinging back, which removes the hamstring stretch entirely.
Rounding the lower back as you bend forward, which is the exact pattern a hinge teach should fix.
Bending the knees too much, which turns the lift into a half-squat instead of a clean hinge.
Hyperextending the back at the top instead of finishing in a tall, neutral standing position.
benefits: Teaches a safe hip-hinge pattern with no equipment.
Activates the glutes and hamstrings before loaded hinge work.
Builds lower-back awareness for safer lifting in any program.

name: Bodyweight Deficit Reverse Lunge
summary: A reverse lunge stepped off a low platform so the rear knee drops below the front foot, done with empty hands.
instructions: Stand on a low platform with both feet on top and the torso upright.
Brace the trunk and clasp the hands at the chest or let them hang.
Step one leg straight back and plant the ball of that foot on the floor.
Bend both knees until the rear knee drops below the level of the front foot.
Keep the front foot flat on the platform and most of the weight on that leg.
Drive through the front foot to return to standing on the platform, then switch sides.
mistakes: Pushing off the rear foot so the front leg stops doing the work.
Letting the front knee cave inward as you step back.
Taking too short a step so the rear knee cannot drop below the platform.
Crashing the rear knee into the floor instead of stopping just above it.
benefits: Increases hip range compared with a floor reverse lunge, which loads the glutes more.
Stays knee-friendlier than a forward lunge because the step is backward.
Builds single-leg strength and balance with no external load.

name: Bodyweight Donkey Calf Raise
summary: A bent-over calf raise that targets the gastrocnemius through a deep stretch — the old-school calf builder, no machine needed.
instructions: Stand with the balls of your feet on the edge of a step or low platform, heels hanging off the back.
Hinge forward at the hips and place your hands on a sturdy surface in front of you for support.
Keep your back flat and your legs nearly straight with just a soft bend in the knees.
Lower your heels slowly below the platform until you feel a deep stretch through the calves.
Press through the balls of your feet to rise up as high as possible onto your toes.
Squeeze the calves hard at the top, then lower under control over 2 to 3 seconds and repeat.
mistakes: Bending the knees too much, which shifts the work off the gastrocnemius onto the soleus.
Cutting the range short and skipping the deep heel stretch where most of the growth happens.
Bouncing the reps instead of lowering under control — kills the time-under-tension on the calves.
Rounding the back in the bent-over position, which puts strain on the lower back over volume.
benefits: Builds calf size by loading the gastrocnemius in a deep stretch.
Trains the calves through a fuller range than standing variations.
Develops calf shape with no machine needed.

name: Bodyweight Elevated Push Up
summary: A push-up with hands raised on a bench or box that scales the difficulty down — the cleanest beginner push-up regression.
instructions: Place your hands on a sturdy bench or box slightly wider than shoulder width.
Walk your feet back until your body forms a straight line from head to heels at an incline.
Brace your core, squeeze your glutes, and pull your shoulder blades back and down.
Lower your chest toward the bench under control with elbows tracked at about 45 degrees from your torso.
Pause briefly when your chest is just above the bench, keeping full-body tension throughout.
Press back up explosively through the palms until your arms lock out, then reset for the next rep.
mistakes: Letting the hips sag down or piking up, which breaks the straight body line and loads the back.
Flaring the elbows out wide, which strains the front shoulders and reduces chest engagement.
Cutting the depth short instead of bringing the chest close to the bench, which removes most of the chest work.
Using a surface that is too high — turns the push-up into a near-standing motion with little load.
benefits: Builds pressing strength at a scalable, beginner-friendly load.
Develops chest, triceps, and front-shoulder size with no equipment.
Teaches clean push-up mechanics before progressing to floor push-ups.

name: Bodyweight Hip Abduction
summary: A standing side-leg lift that moves one straight leg away from the body while the supporting leg and upright torso stay steady.
instructions: Stand upright with your feet close together and your weight balanced.
Bring your hands together in front of your chest, as shown in the clip.
Shift your weight onto one leg without leaning the torso sideways.
Keep the other knee straight and lift that leg out to the side.
Keep your toes facing forward and stop before the pelvis hikes or turns.
Return the moving foot smoothly toward the starting position and repeat with control.
mistakes: Leaning the torso away from the moving leg to gain extra height.
Turning the knee and toes outward instead of keeping the leg facing forward.
Hiking the pelvis or rotating the body during the lift.
Swinging the leg quickly instead of controlling the lift and return.
benefits: Practises moving the leg sideways from the hip.
Loads the outer hip using the weight of the moving leg.
Combines hip movement with control of an upright standing position.

name: Bodyweight Knee Push Ups
summary: A push-up done from the knees that drops the load — the first regression that lets beginners actually train the push pattern.
instructions: Start on all fours with hands placed slightly wider than shoulder width on the floor.
Walk your hands forward and lower your hips so your body forms a straight line from head to knees.
Brace your core, squeeze your glutes, and pull your shoulder blades back and down.
Lower your chest toward the floor under control with elbows tracked at about 45 degrees from your torso.
Pause briefly with your chest just above the floor, keeping full-body tension throughout.
Press back up through the palms until your arms lock out, then reset for the next rep.
mistakes: Letting the hips pike up so the body bends at the waist, which removes most of the chest work.
Flaring the elbows out to 90 degrees, which strains the front shoulders and reduces chest engagement.
Cutting the depth short and bouncing off a partial range, which kills the strength carryover.
Sitting the hips back toward the heels — turns a push-up into a half-rep stretch.
benefits: Builds chest and triceps strength at a beginner-friendly load.
Teaches clean push-up mechanics before progressing to full push-ups.
Trains the upper body anywhere with no equipment.

name: Bodyweight Reverse Lunge
summary: A single-leg lunge stepping backward — builds the glutes and quads while staying easy on the front knee.
instructions: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart and your hands on your hips or at your chest.
Take a long step back with one leg, planting the ball of the back foot down lightly.
Lower the back knee straight down toward the floor while keeping the front shin near vertical.
Drop until the back knee is just above the ground and the front thigh is roughly parallel to the floor.
Drive through the heel of the front foot to push yourself back up to a tall standing position.
Repeat on the same leg for the prescribed reps, then switch sides without losing form.
mistakes: Stepping back too short, which puts the load on the front knee instead of the front glute.
Letting the front knee cave inward instead of tracking over the foot.
Pushing off the back foot instead of driving through the front heel — robs the working leg of work.
Slamming the back knee into the floor instead of lowering it under control.
benefits: Builds the glutes, quads, and hamstrings through a single-leg pattern.
Easier on the knees than forward lunges, making it accessible for more users.
Trains balance and stability without weights.

name: Bodyweight Russian Twist
summary: A seated rotational core exercise that twists side to side — the most recognizable oblique builder in any ab program.
instructions: Sit on the floor with your knees bent and your feet flat on the ground in front of you.
Lean back until your torso is at about a 45-degree angle and brace your core hard.
Lift your feet a few inches off the floor and balance on your sit bones with shins parallel to the ground.
Clasp your hands together in front of your chest and rotate your torso to one side under control.
Tap your hands lightly to the floor beside your hip, feeling the oblique on that side contract.
Rotate smoothly to the other side and tap, alternating for the prescribed reps without dropping the feet.
mistakes: Just swinging the arms side to side without rotating the torso — loads the shoulders, not the core.
Rounding the back instead of staying tall through the spine, which strains the lower back.
Letting the feet drop to the floor every rep, which breaks the constant core tension.
Rushing the tempo instead of pausing on each side — turns a controlled twist into momentum-only work.
benefits: Builds the obliques and abdominals through the rotation pattern.
Develops core endurance and rotational strength.
Trains the core anywhere with no equipment needed.

name: Bodyweight Spinal Jefferson Curl
summary: A slow, segmented forward fold that mobilizes the entire spine — the gymnastics-staple flexibility drill for stiff backs.
instructions: Stand tall on a flat surface with feet hip-width apart and arms hanging in front of your thighs.
Tuck your chin to your chest and start rolling down slowly, one vertebra at a time.
Continue folding forward through the upper back, then mid-back, then lower back as you descend.
Let your arms hang relaxed in front of your shins and reach for the floor without straining.
Pause briefly at the bottom, feeling the stretch through the entire back of the body.
Reverse the motion by rolling back up segment by segment until you stand fully tall again.
mistakes: Folding from the hips only instead of rounding the spine — defeats the entire point of the drill.
Bending the knees too much, which removes the hamstring stretch and shortens the load on the back.
Going too heavy too soon — this is a mobility tool, not a strength lift.
Snapping back up to standing instead of rolling up segment by segment under control.
benefits: Improves spinal mobility through a full forward-fold range.
Stretches the hamstrings, glutes, and entire back of the body.
Builds resilience and control in a flexed spine position.

name: Bodyweight Squat
summary: The foundational squat pattern done with just bodyweight — the first leg exercise in any program and the test of clean mechanics.
instructions: Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart and your toes pointed slightly outward.
Brace your core, lift your chest, and extend your arms straight out for balance.
Sit your hips back and down as if lowering into a chair, keeping your weight in your heels.
Lower until your thighs are at least parallel to the floor, with knees tracking over your toes.
Keep your chest tall and your spine neutral throughout the descent — no rounding at the bottom.
Drive through your heels to stand back up, squeezing your glutes hard at the top of the rep.
mistakes: Letting the knees cave inward, which weakens the squat and loads the knee joint badly.
Squatting straight down instead of sitting the hips back, which puts all the work on the knees.
Lifting the heels off the floor at the bottom, which kills balance and reduces glute drive.
Cutting the depth short and squatting only halfway — robs the lift of glute and quad work.
benefits: Builds the quads, glutes, and inner thighs with no equipment.
Teaches the foundational squat pattern for every loaded variation.
Improves lower-body mobility and balance in any setting.

name: Bodyweight Squat to Stand
summary: A mobility drill that folds forward, grips the toes, drops into a deep squat, then lifts the hips back into the fold.
instructions: Stand with the feet about shoulder-width apart and the toes slightly out.
Hinge forward, keep the legs nearly straight, and grip the toes of each foot.
Bend the knees and drop the hips into a deep squat while lifting the chest, hands still on the toes.
Push the knees out with the elbows if they fit inside the thighs, and keep the heels down.
Straighten the legs slowly and lift the hips back into the forward fold without releasing the toes.
Cycle between the squat and the fold for the desired reps, then stand up.
mistakes: Rounding the lower back hard in the fold instead of hinging from the hips.
Letting the heels lift, which collapses the squat and loses the ankle range.
Releasing the toes at the bottom so the drill becomes an ordinary squat.
Forcing a depth the hips and ankles cannot own, which tucks the pelvis.
benefits: Links a hamstring fold to a deep squat so both ranges are trained in one cycle.
Needs no equipment and little space, so it fits warm-ups anywhere.
Preps the hips, ankles, and posterior chain for later squatting.

name: Bounds
summary: An alternating-leg horizontal bound: an exaggerated running stride that covers distance with a long, springy flight.
instructions: Stand tall with the feet close, one foot slightly ahead, and the arms relaxed.
Lean forward a little and load the lead leg without sitting into a deep squat.
Drive that leg into the floor and bound forward, cycling the other knee through.
Land on the opposite foot on the ball of the foot, then bound again immediately.
Keep the torso upright and the legs relatively long rather than tucking into a hop.
Continue alternating legs for the desired distance or number of contacts.
mistakes: Sitting into a deep squat on each takeoff, which turns the bound into a jump squat.
Landing stiff-legged with a locked knee, which dumps the impact into the joint.
Letting the hips twist so each bound becomes a shuffle instead of a straight stride.
Pausing on every landing instead of using the landing as the next takeoff.
benefits: Trains horizontal spring and stride power that transfers to sprinting and jumping.
Uses only bodyweight, so it fits field and studio plyometric blocks.
Bridges a two-foot broad jump and actual running without adding a box.

name: Box Jump
summary: An explosive jump from the floor onto a box — the clean way to train lower-body power without high-impact landings.
instructions: Stand a comfortable distance in front of a sturdy box with feet shoulder-width apart.
Drop into a quarter squat by sitting your hips back and swinging your arms behind you.
Explode upward by driving through the floor and swinging your arms forward and up.
Pull your knees up underneath you in mid-air and aim to land softly on top of the box.
Land in a soft quarter squat with both feet flat on the box and your chest tall.
Stand fully tall on top of the box, then step down one leg at a time and reset for the next rep.
mistakes: Jumping down from the box instead of stepping down — adds unnecessary impact to the knees over volume.
Landing with stiff legs and a flat impact instead of absorbing softly into a quarter squat.
Choosing a box too tall and barely clearing it, which leads to scraped shins and missed reps.
Using too much arm swing without leg drive — turns a power lift into an arm-thrown jump.
benefits: Builds explosive lower-body power for sport and athletic performance.
Trains reactive strength with reduced landing impact.
Develops glute, quad, and calf power through triple extension.

name: Bradford/Rocky Presses
summary: A standing barbell press that cycles the bar from the front of the neck to behind it, keeping constant tension on the delts.
instructions: Unrack a barbell at collarbone height with a pronated grip just outside the shoulders.
Stand with the feet about shoulder-width apart, brace the trunk, and tuck the chin.
Press the bar about three-quarters of the way to lockout; do not fully straighten the elbows.
Lower the bar behind the neck under control to the base of the neck.
Press again to the same three-quarter height, then lower the bar back to the front rack.
Keep cycling front to back without using the legs to drive the bar.
mistakes: Locking the elbows out at the top, which rests the bar and dumps the tension.
Using a knee dip to push the bar, which turns the drill into a push press.
Leaning the torso back so the lower back takes the load.
Forcing a narrow behind-the-neck path when the shoulders cannot own that position.
benefits: Keeps the delts under tension by cycling the bar front to back without a full lockout.
Trains both a front-rack press and a behind-the-neck press in one movement.
Uses a standard barbell, so it fits barbell shoulder collections.

name: Breaststroke Swim
summary: Prone simultaneous-stroke swimming that pairs a wide sweeping arm pull with a whip kick driven by the inner thighs.
instructions: Float face down with your body straight and arms extended in front of you.
Sweep both hands outward then back toward the midline in a circle, keeping the elbows high.
Lift your head and shoulders to inhale as the arms complete the pull.
Recover the hands together ahead of your shoulders, then shoot them forward.
Draw your heels toward your seat, turn your feet out and whip them back together.
Hold the streamlined glide until speed drops, then start the next cycle.
mistakes: Pulling too wide and too far back, which stalls the stroke and overloads the shoulders.
Kicking with the feet pointed instead of turned out, which removes most of the propulsion.
Cutting the glide short, so stroke rate rises and efficiency falls.
Lifting the head too early, which drops the hips and drags the body line.
benefits: Builds a low-impact aerobic pattern with a clear, teachable rhythm.
Loads the inner thigh and hip musculature harder than the other strokes.
Allows a breath every cycle, which makes pacing straightforward for beginners.

name: Broad Jump
summary: A two-foot standing long jump: load the hips, swing the arms, and project the body forward as far as possible.
instructions: Stand with the feet about shoulder-width apart and the toes just behind a start line.
Swing both arms back as you hinge the hips and bend the knees to load the legs.
Drive the arms forward and extend the hips, knees, and ankles to jump out, not just up.
Bring the feet forward in the air so you can land under the hips.
Land on both feet with the knees and hips bent, and absorb the impact quietly.
Reset the stance before the next jump; do not bounce immediately into another max effort.
mistakes: Jumping only upward so the landing is under the takeoff instead of ahead of it.
Landing with locked knees, which dumps the impact into the joints.
Letting the knees cave inward on takeoff or landing.
Cutting the arm swing, which costs distance and timing.
benefits: Trains horizontal power from a two-foot stance with no run-up and no box.
Is easy to measure, so it fits testing and athletic-content pages.
Loads the posterior chain and core in a short, intense burst.

name: Broomstick Pass-Throughs
summary: A shoulder mobility drill that rotates a wide-grip dowel from in front of the thighs, over the head, and behind the hips.
instructions: Stand tall with the feet about shoulder-width apart and hold a straight dowel in front of the thighs.
Take a wide overhand grip, wider than the shoulders, with both elbows straight.
Brace the trunk so the ribs stay stacked over the pelvis.
Raise the stick in a wide arc over the head, keeping the arms long.
Continue the arc until the stick travels behind the hips as far as the shoulders allow.
Reverse the same path back to the front of the thighs without bending the elbows.
mistakes: Bending the elbows to cheat the stick over the head.
Using a grip so narrow that the shoulders pinch at the top.
Flaring the ribs or leaning back to make the stick clear the head.
Forcing the stick to the lower back through a painful end range.
benefits: Takes the shoulders through a full overhead arc with a simple stick.
Is an easy warm-up for overhead pressing, carrying, and throwing patterns.
Needs only a broom handle or dowel, so it works in home and gym settings.

name: Bulgarian Split Squat
summary: A rear-foot-elevated split squat that punishes one leg at a time — the most effective single-leg builder in any program.
instructions: Stand a stride-length away from a bench and place the top of your back foot on the bench behind you.
Square your hips forward and brace your core with your hands on your hips or at your chest.
Lower your back knee straight down toward the floor while keeping your front shin near vertical.
Drop until the back knee is just above the ground and the front thigh is roughly parallel to the floor.
Keep your weight in the front heel and your chest tall throughout the descent.
Drive through the front heel to push yourself back up, finishing with the front glute squeezed.
mistakes: Standing too close to the bench, which shoves the front knee too far forward and loads the joint.
Letting the front knee cave inward instead of tracking over the foot.
Pushing off the back foot instead of driving through the front heel — robs the front leg of work.
Twisting the hips to compensate for balance instead of staying square — kills the unilateral training.
benefits: Builds single-leg strength in the glutes, quads, and hamstrings.
Exposes and corrects left-right strength imbalances.
Improves hip stability and balance under load.

name: Burpee
summary: A squat-thrust into a push-up into a jump — the full-body conditioning move that hits everything in one rep.
instructions: Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart, arms relaxed at your sides, and core braced.
Drop into a low squat and place your hands on the floor just in front of your feet.
Kick or step both feet back so you land in a high plank position with arms straight.
Lower your chest to the floor in a controlled push-up, then press back up to the high plank.
Jump or step both feet back up under your hips into the squat position.
Explode upward into a jump with arms reaching overhead, land softly, and reset for the next rep.
mistakes: Skipping the push-up at the bottom and turning the burpee into a squat-thrust-jump instead.
Sagging the hips in the plank position, which strains the lower back over volume.
Landing the jump with stiff legs instead of absorbing softly into a quarter squat.
Going so fast that form collapses — turns a conditioning lift into a sloppy injury risk.
benefits: Trains full-body strength and conditioning in a single movement.
Spikes the heart rate fast for efficient cardio work.
Builds explosive power, pressing strength, and core endurance at once.

name: Butterfly Swim
summary: Simultaneous double-arm swimming timed to a dolphin kick, with the body undulating around the hips through every cycle.
instructions: Start prone with your body long and both arms extended in front of you.
Press both hands out and down together, keeping the elbows high.
Drive both arms back past your hips to finish the pull.
Sweep both arms over the water simultaneously into the next entry.
Beat both legs together in a dolphin kick timed to the entry and the finish.
Breathe forward once every second or third cycle as the arms clear the water.
mistakes: Lifting the head high to breathe, which sinks the hips and stalls the recovery.
Pulling with the arms only, so the body wave and kick stop contributing.
Mistiming the second kick, which leaves the arms to drag the body through the entry.
Swimming long sets while fatigued, exactly when shoulder mechanics start to break down.
benefits: Loads back, chest and shoulders through the widest range of the four strokes.
Demands whole-body timing between the arm pull, kick and body wave.
Delivers the highest intensity of the competitive strokes for short efforts.

name: Cable 30 Degree Shrug
summary: A cable shrug performed at a 30-degree angle that loads the upper traps along their natural fiber line — the smarter shrug variation.
instructions: Set the cable at the lowest pulley setting and attach a straight bar or rope handle.
Stand a foot or two back from the cable and grip the handle with arms straight.
Lean your torso forward at about a 30-degree angle, keeping a flat back and braced core.
Let your shoulders relax forward and down so the cable pulls your traps into a stretch.
Shrug your shoulders up and slightly back along the angle of the cable, squeezing the traps hard.
Lower the weight back down under control over 2 to 3 seconds and repeat for high reps.
mistakes: Standing fully upright, which turns the lift into a regular straight-up shrug.
Bending the elbows instead of keeping the arms straight — loads the biceps, not the traps.
Rounding the lower back in the leaned-over position, which strains the spine over volume.
Using too much weight and rolling the shoulders forward instead of shrugging up and back.
benefits: Builds upper-trap size along the natural fiber direction.
Develops back thickness and a stronger upper-back silhouette.
Trains the traps through a fuller range than standing dumbbell shrugs.

name: Cable Bar Curl
summary: A two-handed cable curl using a straight bar attachment that hammers the biceps with constant tension from bottom to top.
instructions: Set the pulley to the lowest position and attach a straight bar, then grip it underhand at shoulder width.
Step back so the cable has tension at full arm extension and stand tall with your elbows tucked at your ribs.
Curl the bar up toward your shoulders by bending only at the elbows, keeping the upper arms locked in place.
Squeeze the biceps hard at the top with the bar a few inches from your collarbone.
Lower the bar slowly over 2 to 3 seconds, fighting the cable tension all the way back to full extension.
Reset your stance and repeat for 10 to 15 controlled reps without using your back or hips.
mistakes: Swinging the torso back to fling the bar up, which steals load from the biceps and risks lower-back strain.
Letting the elbows drift forward at the top, turning the curl into a partial front raise.
Cutting the lockout short at the bottom, missing the long-head stretch where most growth lives.
Rushing the lowering phase, which throws away the highest-tension half of the rep where the biceps grow most.
benefits: Builds biceps size and peak with constant cable tension.
Trains both heads of the biceps through a full range of motion.
Reinforces strict elbow mechanics for cleaner curl form.

name: Cable Bar Face Pull
summary: A high-cable face pull using a straight bar that targets the rear delts and upper-back posture muscles.
instructions: Set the pulley above head height and attach a straight bar, then grip it overhand at shoulder width.
Step back until the cable has tension and stand with feet hip-width apart and a slight forward lean.
Pull the bar toward your forehead with the elbows flaring wide and high, leading with the back of the upper arms.
Squeeze your rear delts and upper back at the end of the pull, keeping your wrists in line with your forearms.
Slowly let the bar travel back to full arm extension over 2 to 3 seconds, keeping the chest tall.
Repeat for 12 to 20 reps, prioritizing the squeeze and elbow path over loading heavy weight.
mistakes: Pulling the bar too low toward the chin or chest, which turns the lift into a row and loses the rear-delt focus.
Letting the elbows drop instead of leading high and wide, swapping rear-delt work for biceps engagement.
Leaning back hard to use bodyweight as a counterweight instead of pulling cleanly with the back.
Loading too heavy and shrugging the traps up, hiding the rear delts under upper-trap dominance.
benefits: Builds the rear delts and upper-back muscles that balance pressing work.
Reinforces healthy shoulder posture for desk workers and lifters alike.
Strengthens the small stabilizers around the shoulder blade for joint health.

name: Cable Bar Pushdown
summary: A standing triceps pushdown using a straight bar attachment — the most efficient way to isolate the triceps with cables.
instructions: Set the pulley to the highest position and attach a straight bar, then grip it overhand at shoulder width.
Step close to the stack and tuck your elbows tight against your ribs with your forearms parallel to the floor.
Press the bar straight down by extending your elbows fully, keeping the upper arms locked in place.
Squeeze the triceps hard at the bottom with the arms straight and the bar near your thighs.
Let the bar travel back up slowly over 2 seconds, stopping when your forearms are parallel to the floor.
Repeat for 10 to 15 reps, keeping a tall torso and avoiding any forward lean to muscle the bar down.
mistakes: Letting the elbows flare forward and away from the ribs, turning the lift into a chest-driven press.
Leaning the torso forward to push down with bodyweight, which steals load from the triceps.
Cutting the lockout short, missing the strongest contraction at the bottom of the movement.
Bouncing the weight up at the top instead of controlling the return, throwing away half the working set.
benefits: Builds triceps size and lockout strength with isolated tension.
Targets all three heads of the triceps through a full range of motion.
Reinforces stable elbow mechanics for stronger pressing lifts.

name: Cable Bench Chest Fly
summary: A bench-supported cable fly that puts the chest under deep stretch with constant tension top to bottom.
instructions: Position a flat bench between two cable stations and set both pulleys to the lowest position with single handles.
Lie back on the bench and press both handles up over your chest with a slight bend in your elbows.
Lower the handles out to your sides in a wide arc, keeping the elbow angle locked the whole way down.
Stop when your hands are roughly level with your shoulders and you feel a deep stretch across the chest.
Bring the handles back together in the same arc by squeezing the chest, finishing with the hands meeting above you.
Pause at the top with a hard chest squeeze, then repeat for 10 to 15 controlled reps.
mistakes: Bending the elbows mid-rep, which turns the fly into a sloppy press and shifts load off the chest.
Dropping the hands too far below shoulder level, overstretching the front shoulders and risking joint strain.
Rushing the lowering phase, where most of the chest-building tension lives.
Letting the shoulders roll forward off the bench, losing the stable platform that keeps the chest loaded.
benefits: Builds chest size with constant cable tension through a full arc.
Develops the inner-chest squeeze that pressing alone misses.
Trains the chest in deep stretch for stronger hypertrophy stimulus.

name: Cable Bench Press
summary: A bench-supported cable press that trains the chest and triceps with smooth, constant tension through the full press.
instructions: Place a flat bench between two cable stations and set both pulleys to the lowest position with single handles.
Lie back on the bench and press both handles up so your arms are extended directly over your chest.
Lower the handles to chest level with the elbows tracking at about 60 to 75 degrees from your torso.
Pause briefly at the bottom with a deep chest stretch and a tight upper back pressed into the bench.
Press both handles back up in a slight arc until they meet above your chest at full arm extension.
Squeeze the chest at the top and repeat for 8 to 12 controlled reps.
mistakes: Letting the elbows flare wide to 90 degrees, which strains the front shoulders and reduces chest engagement.
Pressing the handles in different paths, causing one side to dominate and creating uneven loading.
Cutting the lockout short, missing the chest-squeeze position at the top of the press.
Lifting the head or hips off the bench for leverage, which destabilizes the press.
benefits: Builds chest and triceps strength with smooth, constant tension.
Removes the lockout dead spot found in barbell pressing.
Allows independent arm work to expose and fix side-to-side imbalances.

name: Cable Bench Straight Leg Kickback
summary: A bench-supported cable kickback that isolates the glutes with a straight-leg drive against constant cable tension.
instructions: Attach a cable cuff to your ankle and set the pulley to the lowest position, then face the cable stack.
Stand a few feet back from the stack and rest your forearms on a flat bench in front of you.
Brace your core and start with the working leg lightly forward so the cable has tension at rest.
Drive the straight leg back and up by squeezing the glute, finishing in line with or slightly above your torso.
Pause at the top for a hard glute squeeze, keeping your hips level and your lower back neutral.
Lower the leg under control back to the start, then repeat for 12 to 15 reps before switching sides.
mistakes: Arching the lower back to throw the leg higher, which loads the spine instead of the glutes.
Letting the working hip rotate open, which lets the lower back take over the movement.
Bending the knee mid-rep, swapping glute work for hamstring engagement.
Rushing the return phase and letting the cable yank the leg forward instead of controlling the descent.
benefits: Isolates and builds the glutes without involving the quads.
Strengthens hip extension for sport, sprinting, and heavier hinges.
Shapes the glutes from a different angle than squats and deadlifts.

name: Cable Chest Press
summary: A standing cable press that trains the chest, triceps, and front delts through a horizontal push pattern with constant tension.
instructions: Set both cable pulleys to chest height and grip a single handle in each hand with an overhand grip.
Step forward into a staggered stance with one foot ahead of the other and brace your core hard.
Start with the handles by your chest, elbows tucked at about 60 to 75 degrees from your torso.
Press both handles forward in a slight arc until your arms meet at full extension in front of your chest.
Squeeze the chest at the top, then return the handles slowly to the start over 2 to 3 seconds.
Repeat for 10 to 15 reps, keeping the torso upright and the staggered stance locked the whole set.
mistakes: Leaning the torso forward to push the handles instead of pressing cleanly with the chest and arms.
Letting the elbows flare wide to shoulder height, which strains the front shoulders.
Allowing one arm to lead the press, creating uneven loading and shoulder asymmetry over time.
Cutting the range short on the way back, missing the chest stretch that drives growth.
benefits: Builds chest, triceps, and front-delt strength in a standing position.
Trains the core to brace against horizontal load — useful for sport.
Removes the lockout dead spot found in barbell pressing.

name: Cable Chop
summary: A standing diagonal cable pull across the body, with both hands sharing a handle and the obliques highlighted through the turn.
instructions: Set the cable above shoulder height and stand sideways to the stack.
