Hold one handle with both hands and take a comfortably wide stance.
Brace the trunk with the hands near the high-pulley side.
Turn smoothly while guiding the handle down across the body.
Finish near the opposite hip without pulling the shoulders upward.
Control the return to the high starting position before repeating.
mistakes: Moving the handle vertically instead of across the body.
Jerking the handle with the arms while losing trunk control.
Allowing the cable to pull the body back abruptly.
Arching the lower back to reach a larger range.
benefits: Trains control of a diagonal movement against resistance.
Engages the abdominal complex during rotation.
Provides a visible demonstration of cross-body cable loading.

name: Cable Decline Bench Press
summary: A decline cable press performed on a bench that targets the lower chest with smooth constant tension.
instructions: Set a decline bench between two cable stations with both pulleys at the lowest position and single handles attached.
Lock your feet under the pads and lie back, then press both handles up over your lower chest.
Lower the handles to chest level with the elbows tracking at about 60 to 75 degrees from your torso.
Pause briefly at the bottom with a deep chest stretch, keeping the upper back tight against the bench.
Press the handles back up in a slight arc until they meet above the lower chest at full extension.
Squeeze the chest hard at the top and repeat for 8 to 12 reps with controlled tempo.
mistakes: Letting the elbows flare wide, which strains the front shoulders and pulls focus off the lower chest.
Rushing the descent and missing the deep chest stretch that drives hypertrophy.
Pressing the handles unevenly, creating side-to-side imbalances over time.
Lifting the hips off the bench for leverage, which destabilizes the press and risks back strain.
benefits: Targets the lower chest with constant cable tension.
Builds a thicker lower-chest line for balanced chest development.
Removes the lockout dead spot found in barbell decline pressing.

name: Cable External Rotation
summary: A cable rotator cuff drill that rotates the forearm away from the stomach with the elbow fixed against the ribs.
instructions: Set a cable pulley to about waist height and attach a single handle.
Stand side on so the working arm is furthest from the machine, and take the handle across your body.
Tuck the working elbow against your ribs and bend it to ninety degrees.
Brace your trunk and rotate the forearm outward, away from your stomach, without moving the elbow.
Pause for about one second at the end of the rotation.
Let the cable draw the hand back slowly to the start, then repeat and switch sides.
mistakes: Letting the elbow leave the ribs, which converts the rep into a row driven by the back.
Turning the torso away from the machine, which produces range the shoulder never generated.
Selecting a heavy plate, which recruits the lats and rear deltoid instead of the cuff.
Releasing the eccentric quickly, which discards the phase where the cuff adapts most.
benefits: Holds tension on the external rotators through the whole range thanks to the cable.
Strengthens the cuff stabilizers that protect the shoulder during pressing and overhead work.
Sets up in seconds on any adjustable stack, so it fits into warm-ups without disruption.

name: Cable Front Raise
summary: A two-handed front raise with the cable running between your legs, holding the front deltoid under load from the bottom up.
instructions: Set a cable pulley to its lowest position and attach a straight bar or rope handle.
Stand facing away from the stack with the cable running between your legs and your feet shoulder-width apart.
Grip the handle with both hands using an overhand grip and let it rest near your thighs.
Brace your abs and raise both arms straight in front of you with a slight bend in the elbows.
Stop when your hands reach shoulder height and pause briefly.
Lower the handle back toward your thighs under control and repeat.
mistakes: Leaning back to start the rep, which uses the trunk instead of the front deltoid.
Raising the hands well above shoulder height, which hands the work to the traps.
Bouncing at the top and dropping the stack, which throws away the constant tension the cable is there for.
Stacking it on top of heavy pressing, which piles yet more volume on an already busy anterior deltoid.
benefits: The cable keeps tension on the front deltoid at the bottom where dumbbells go slack.
A single-joint movement that adds shoulder volume without more overhead pressing.
The fixed line of pull makes the rep easy to standardize across a program.

name: Cable High-to-Low Fly
summary: Standing cable fly that sweeps both handles down and together from high pulleys to load the lower chest.
instructions: Set both cable pulleys to their highest position and select a light load on each side.
Take one handle in each hand with a neutral grip and step forward into a split stance.
Brace your abdominals, hold your torso upright, and keep a slight bend in both elbows.
Sweep both hands down and together in a wide arc until they meet in front of your hips.
Hold the squeeze for a beat without letting the two handles touch.
Let your arms open back out under control until you feel a stretch across the chest, then repeat.
mistakes: Bending and extending the elbows turns the fly into a press, so the triceps take load the chest should carry.
Leaning the torso forward over the front foot increases shoulder joint stress and usually means the load is too heavy.
Banging the handles together at the bottom lets the pecs unload at the point of peak contraction.
Squeezing the handles hard pulls the forearms and biceps in first and blunts the chest contraction.
benefits: Holds tension on the pectorals through the full arc, including the shortened position.
Emphasizes the lower chest through a downward adduction path that flat pressing does not reproduce.
Needs no spotter and no bar to unrack, so it programs safely at the end of a session.

name: Cable Hip Abduction
summary: A standing cable exercise that lifts one straight leg out to the side, isolating the hip abductors.
instructions: Attach an ankle strap to the lowest setting on a cable pulley.
Fasten the strap to the ankle furthest from the machine and stand side on.
Hold the frame for balance with your feet about shoulder width apart.
Brace your abdominals and keep the working knee straight.
Sweep the strapped leg away from the midline with the heel leading the path.
Pause briefly, lower under control against the cable and repeat.
mistakes: Swinging the leg with momentum, which removes tension from the gluteus medius.
Leaning the torso away from the machine, so the trunk moves instead of the hip.
Turning the toe upward, which recruits the hip flexors instead of the abductors.
Lifting past the point of strong contraction, which shifts work to the lower back.
benefits: Isolates the gluteus medius and minimus without a compound lift masking them.
Trains the pelvic stability that single leg movement and running depend on.
Loads hip abduction smoothly through the whole range with cable tension.

name: Cable Incline Bench Press
summary: An incline cable press that targets the upper chest and triceps with constant tension through every inch of the press.
instructions: Set an incline bench to about 30 to 45 degrees between two cable stations with low pulleys and single handles.
Sit back into the bench and press both handles up so the arms are extended over the upper chest.
Lower the handles to upper-chest level with the elbows tracking at about 60 to 75 degrees from your torso.
Pause at the bottom with a deep stretch across the upper chest and a tight upper back.
Press the handles back up in a slight arc until they meet above the upper chest at full arm extension.
Squeeze the upper chest at the top and repeat for 8 to 12 controlled reps.
mistakes: Setting the bench too steep, which turns the press into a shoulder-dominant lift.
Letting the elbows flare wide, straining the front shoulders and reducing upper-chest engagement.
Pressing too fast and skipping the stretch, missing the highest-tension portion of the rep.
Lifting the hips off the bench for leverage, which destabilizes the press.
benefits: Builds the upper chest with constant cable tension.
Develops the upper-chest shelf for a fuller, more balanced chest.
Removes the lockout dead spot found in barbell incline pressing.

name: Cable Kickback
summary: Standing single leg hip extension against a low cable that isolates the glutes through a controlled range.
instructions: Attach an ankle cuff to a low pulley and fasten it around one ankle.
Face the stack and hold the frame with both hands for balance.
Step back until the cable is taut and shift your weight onto the standing leg.
Brace your abs and keep a small bend in the standing knee.
Drive the working leg back and up by squeezing the glute, keeping the hips square.
Return the leg forward under control, finish the set, then swap sides.
mistakes: Arching the lower back to gain range, which moves the work from the glute to the spine.
Rotating the hips open each rep, so the leg travels further without more glute work.
Swinging the leg with momentum, which removes tension from the glute at the top.
Loading too heavy, so the torso leans forward and the standing leg does the stabilizing.
benefits: Isolates hip extension so the glutes work without the quads sharing the load.
Cable tension stays constant through the range, unlike a bodyweight kickback.
Trains one side at a time, which exposes side to side strength differences.

name: Cable Low Single Arm Lateral Raise
summary: A one-arm lateral raise from a low cable pulley, with the cable crossing the body to load the side of the shoulder.
instructions: Set a cable pulley to its lowest position and attach a single handle.
Stand side-on to the stack so the working arm is the one furthest from the pulley.
Reach across your body and take the handle with a neutral grip, keeping the chest tall and hips level.
Brace your abs and press both feet into the floor.
Raise the working arm out to the side with a slight elbow bend until it is level with the floor.
Hold for a second, lower slowly back across your body, then finish the set and switch arms.
mistakes: Swinging the torso away from the stack, which replaces deltoid work with a body swing.
Shrugging as the arm rises, which moves the load up into the upper traps.
Letting the handle drop back fast, which wastes the loaded stretch the low pulley creates.
Raising past shoulder height, which shifts the work off the side of the deltoid.
benefits: Working one arm at a time exposes side-to-side differences the two-arm version hides.
The low pulley keeps the side of the deltoid loaded at the bottom of the range.
Trial evidence puts cable lateral raises on a par with dumbbells for lateral deltoid growth.

name: Cable Low-to-High Fly
summary: Standing cable fly driven upward and inward from low pulleys so the upper chest does the adduction work.
instructions: Set both pulleys to their lowest position and select a light load on each side.
Grip a handle in each hand with palms turned slightly upward and step forward into a staggered stance.
Stand tall, brace your abdominals, and keep a soft bend in both elbows.
Drive both hands up and inward on a forty-five degree line until they meet at chest or face height.
Pause briefly at the top and hold the chest contraction without clashing the handles.
Lower your arms back down and out under control, then repeat for the prescribed reps.
mistakes: Leaning back to help the hands travel upward turns the lift into a shoulder raise and takes the chest out of it.
Letting the elbows flex and extend converts the fly into an incline press and moves load to the triceps.
Driving too high with a heavy stack overloads the front of the shoulder joint and provokes pain there.
Losing the abdominal brace lets the lower back arch, which shortens the working range and stresses the spine.
benefits: Loads the upper chest without an incline bench, which is useful in cable-only gym setups.
Keeps constant cable tension through an arc that ends in full pectoral shortening.
Trains trunk bracing alongside the chest because the stance must resist a forward pull.

name: Cable Overhead Press
summary: A standing cable press overhead that builds the front and side shoulders with smooth constant tension top to bottom.
instructions: Set both cable pulleys to the lowest position and grip a single handle in each hand with an overhand grip.
Step into the cables with a staggered stance, brace your core, and bring the handles to shoulder height.
Start with the elbows tucked roughly 30 degrees in front of the torso and forearms vertical.
Press both handles straight up overhead until the arms lock out with the handles meeting above your head.
Squeeze the shoulders at the top, then lower the handles slowly back to shoulder height over 2 seconds.
Repeat for 8 to 12 controlled reps without leaning back or pressing the hips forward.
mistakes: Leaning back hard to push the handles up, which turns the lift into a standing incline press and risks back strain.
Letting the elbows flare straight out to the sides, which strains the front shoulders.
Cutting the lockout short and missing the strongest contraction at the top.
Pressing too fast on the descent and losing tension before the next rep.
benefits: Builds the front and side shoulders with constant cable tension.
Strengthens the core to brace against vertical overhead load.
Trains a standing pressing pattern that transfers to sport and daily life.

name: Cable Overhead Straight Bar Extensions
summary: A standing overhead triceps extension from a high cable, using a straight bar behind the head with the elbows fixed.
instructions: Clip a straight bar to a high pulley and stand facing away from the stack.
Take an overhand grip on the bar behind the head, about shoulder-width apart.
Hinge the torso slightly forward so the upper arms sit beside the head, parallel to the floor.
Brace the trunk and keep the elbows in place; only the forearms should move.
Extend the elbows until the arms are straight and the bar travels forward.
Bend the elbows under control to return the bar behind the head, then repeat.
mistakes: Letting the elbows flare or drift, which turns the lift into a pullover.
Swinging the torso to move the stack instead of isolating the elbows.
Locking out so hard that the load dumps onto the joints at the top.
Using a grip so narrow or so wide that the wrists fold under the bar.
benefits: Isolates the triceps through a long overhead range with constant cable tension.
Uses a straight bar, so the page is distinct from a rope overhead extension.
Is a beginner cable isolation lift that fits arm-day templates.

name: Cable Pallof Press
summary: A standing anti-rotation drill: hold a chest-height cable side-on and press it out without letting the torso turn.
instructions: Set a single handle on a cable pulley at mid-chest height.
Stand side-on to the stack, take the handle in both hands, and hold it at the center of the chest.
Step out until the cable is taut, with the feet about hip-width and the knees slightly bent.
Brace the trunk so the shoulders and hips face straight ahead.
Press the handle straight out until the elbows are extended, without letting the torso turn.
Pause, then bring the handle back to the chest under control, finish the set, and switch sides.
mistakes: Using so much load that the near shoulder rotates toward the stack.
Letting the hands drift sideways instead of pressing straight from the sternum.
Flaring the ribs or arching the lower back as the arms extend.
Training only one side and skipping the turn-around set.
benefits: Trains the trunk to resist rotation in a standing, athletic stance.
Makes bracing errors easy to see as soon as the hands leave the chest.
Uses a standard cable stack, so it fits gym and app cable-core collections.

name: Cable Pec Fly
summary: A standing cable fly that isolates the chest with constant tension from a deep stretch to a hard squeeze.
instructions: Set both cable pulleys to chest height and grip a single handle in each hand with a slight elbow bend.
Step forward into a staggered stance and lean slightly forward at the hips with a tall chest.
Start with the arms stretched out wide in line with your chest, palms facing forward.
Bring both handles together in a wide arc by squeezing the chest, finishing with hands meeting in front of you.
Pause at the top with a hard chest squeeze, keeping the elbow bend locked the whole way.
Open the arms back out slowly over 2 to 3 seconds and repeat for 12 to 15 reps.
mistakes: Bending the elbows mid-rep, which turns the fly into a sloppy press and loses the chest focus.
Letting the hands drop too far behind the body, overstretching the front shoulders.
Rushing the opening phase, throwing away the slow return where most of the chest tension lives.
Using the torso to swing the handles together instead of squeezing with the chest.
benefits: Isolates the chest with constant cable tension.
Develops the inner-chest squeeze that pressing alone misses.
Loads the chest in deep stretch for stronger hypertrophy stimulus.

name: Cable Pull Through
summary: A cable-loaded hip hinge that pulls resistance forward from between the legs, driving the glutes with little spinal load.
instructions: Attach a rope to the lowest setting on a cable stack and face away from the machine.
Straddle the cable, reach between your legs and take one rope end in each hand.
Walk forward until the cable is taut, then set your feet about shoulder width apart.
Push your hips back and hinge forward with a flat back until the rope passes behind your legs.
Drive the hips forward and squeeze the glutes to stand tall, keeping the arms straight.
Control the return as the cable pulls you back into the hinge, then repeat.
mistakes: Bending the knees into a squat, which shifts the work from the glutes to the quadriceps.
Standing too close to the stack, which leaves no tension at the stretched position.
Pulling the rope with the arms, which turns a hip hinge into a row.
Arching the lower back at lockout instead of finishing with the glutes.
benefits: Loads the glutes and hamstrings without placing compressive load on the spine.
Teaches the hip hinge pattern that deadlifts and kettlebell swings depend on.
Keeps tension constant through the range, which suits higher rep volume work.

name: Cable Rope Face Pulls
summary: A high-cable rope pull to the face that trains the rear delts and upper back — the go-to fix for forward-rolled shoulders.
instructions: Set the cable to slightly above eye level and attach a rope handle at the end of the cable.
Grip the rope with palms facing inward and step back until the cable has tension in the start position.
Plant your feet shoulder-width apart and brace your core, leaning back only slightly to balance the load.
Pull the rope toward your face, leading with the elbows and keeping them high and wide.
Squeeze the rear shoulders and upper back hard at the end of the pull, ears between the rope ends.
Return slowly to the start over 2 to 3 seconds, keeping the elbows up the entire way back.
mistakes: Dropping the elbows low so the lift becomes a row, which loses the rear-delt isolation.
Going too heavy, forcing the body to lean and yank instead of pulling cleanly with the upper back.
Cutting the range short and never bringing the rope to the face, which limits the muscle stretch.
Letting the rope rip back forward and skipping the slow return, where most of the rear-delt work happens.
benefits: Strengthens the rear delts and upper back for healthier, more durable shoulders.
Counteracts forward shoulder posture from desk work and heavy pressing.
Easy to load progressively without straining the joints or low back.

name: Cable Rope Hammer Curl
summary: Standing cable curl on a rope with a neutral grip that loads the biceps, brachialis and forearms together.
instructions: Attach a rope to the low pulley and select a light weight.
Stand facing the stack with your feet about shoulder width apart.
Take one end of the rope in each hand with your palms facing each other.
Tuck your elbows against your sides and brace your abs.
Curl the rope up toward your shoulders, keeping the wrists neutral.
Squeeze at the top, then lower until the arms are almost straight.
mistakes: Letting the elbows drift forward, which turns the curl into a front raise for the shoulders.
Leaning back to start the rep, which uses the hips instead of the elbow flexors.
Rolling the wrists into a palms up position, which drops the brachioradialis out of the movement.
Stopping short at the bottom, so the arm never reaches the loaded stretch the cable provides.
benefits: Trains the biceps, brachialis and brachioradialis in one neutral grip movement.
Keeps cable tension at the bottom of the rep where dumbbells unload.
Neutral wrists usually feel easier on the elbow than a supinated curl.

name: Cable Rope Kneeling Face Pull
summary: A kneeling rope face pull that locks out body english and isolates the rear delts and mid-back.
instructions: Set the pulley above head height and attach a rope, then kneel facing the cable stack on both knees.
Grip the rope with palms facing each other and arms extended forward at eye level with cable tension.
Pull the rope toward your forehead with the elbows flaring wide and high, leading with the upper arms.
Separate the rope ends as you pull, finishing with hands by your ears and elbows in line with your shoulders.
Squeeze the rear delts and mid-back hard at the end of the pull, keeping the chest tall.
Slowly let the rope travel back to the start over 2 seconds and repeat for 12 to 20 reps.
mistakes: Pulling the rope toward the chin or chest, which turns the lift into a row and loses the rear-delt focus.
Letting the elbows drop, swapping rear-delt work for biceps engagement.
Rocking back on the knees to use bodyweight as a counterweight.
Loading too heavy and shrugging the traps up, hiding the rear delts under upper-trap dominance.
benefits: Isolates the rear delts and mid-back without bodyweight cheating.
Reinforces healthy shoulder posture for desk workers and lifters.
Strengthens the small stabilizers around the shoulder blade for joint health.

name: Cable Rope Overhead Tricep Extension
summary: Overhead rope extension from a high pulley that stretches the triceps long head before every elbow extension.
instructions: Attach a rope to a high pulley and select a moderate weight.
Grip both ends with a neutral grip and turn away from the stack.
Take a split stance and bring the rope behind your head with the elbows bent.
Hinge slightly forward at the hips and brace your abs.
Extend your elbows to drive the rope forward and slightly apart.
Stop just short of lockout, then lower back into the stretch under control.
mistakes: Letting the elbows flare and travel, which turns the extension into a press.
Arching the lower back as the cable pulls, which loads the spine instead of the triceps.
Locking out hard at the top, which hands the tension to the elbow joint.
Choosing a weight that pulls you backwards, so the stance rather than the arms controls the rep.
benefits: Loads the triceps long head in a stretched position that pushdowns do not reach.
Constant cable tension through the whole elbow extension range.
Carries over to lockout strength in bench and overhead pressing.

name: Cable Rope Pullover
summary: Straight-arm cable pullover with a rope that extends the shoulders and drives the lats through a long range.
instructions: Attach a rope to a high cable pulley and select a moderate load.
Take one rope end in each hand with a neutral grip and step back until the cable is taut.
Hinge slightly at the hips, brace your abdominals, and set your arms overhead with elbows nearly straight.
Depress your shoulder blades, then pull the rope down in an arc toward your thighs.
Finish with the hands beside your hips and hold the lat contraction for a beat.
Let the rope travel back overhead under control until you feel the lats lengthen, then repeat.
mistakes: Bending the elbows turns the pullover into a triceps pushdown and removes the lats from the movement.
Letting the lower back arch as the arms go overhead shifts the load onto the spine instead of the lats.
Standing too close to the stack cuts the overhead range short, so the lats never reach a stretched position.
Gripping the rope hard and leading with the arms lets the biceps dominate a movement meant for the back.
benefits: Trains the lats through pure shoulder extension with no elbow flexion to steal the work.
Keeps cable tension on the back in the stretched overhead position where free weights go slack.
Teaches shoulder blade depression, which transfers directly to pulldowns and rows.

name: Cable Rope Pushdown
summary: A standing triceps pushdown using a rope attachment that lets the hands separate for a deeper triceps squeeze.
instructions: Set the pulley to the highest position and attach a rope, then grip both ends with palms facing each other.
Step close to the stack and tuck your elbows tight against your ribs with forearms parallel to the floor.
Press both ends of the rope straight down by extending your elbows until your arms are fully locked out.
Pull the rope ends apart at the bottom and rotate the palms down for an extra triceps squeeze.
Let the rope travel back up slowly over 2 seconds, stopping when forearms are parallel to the floor.
Repeat for 10 to 15 reps without leaning forward or letting the elbows drift away from the ribs.
mistakes: Letting the elbows flare forward, turning the lift into a chest-driven press.
Leaning the torso forward to push down with bodyweight, stealing load from the triceps.
Skipping the hand separation at the bottom, missing the deeper long-head contraction.
Bouncing the weight up at the top instead of controlling the return.
benefits: Builds triceps size with a deep contraction at lockout.
Targets the long head of the triceps more than a straight bar pushdown.
Reinforces stable elbow mechanics for stronger pressing lifts.

name: Cable Row Bar Standing Row
summary: A standing cable row using a paired neutral-grip handle to pull toward the torso while the feet stay planted.
instructions: Attach a paired neutral-grip row handle and set the pulley so the cable runs toward your mid-torso.
Hold the upright grips with your palms facing each other and step back until the cable is taut.
Stand with both feet planted and brace your trunk.
Pull the handle toward your torso, moving your elbows back alongside your body.
Return the handle smoothly as your arms extend.
Repeat while keeping your stance steady and avoiding a large backward lean.
mistakes: Leaning far backward to move the handle.
Shrugging the shoulders throughout the pull.
Letting the cable pull the arms forward abruptly.
Changing the grip or attachment so the setup no longer matches the demonstration.
benefits: Loads the back and elbow flexors through a horizontal pull.
Practises a controlled return against cable resistance.
Combines a rowing action with a steady standing stance.

name: Cable Seated Rope Face Pull
summary: A seated rope face pull that removes body english and isolates the rear delts and upper back.
instructions: Set the pulley above head height and attach a rope, then sit on a bench facing the cable stack.
Grip the rope with palms facing each other and arms extended forward at eye level with cable tension.
Sit tall with feet planted, brace your core, and start with no slack in the cable.
Pull the rope toward your forehead with elbows flaring wide and high, leading with the upper arms.
Separate the rope ends and squeeze the rear delts and upper back hard at the end of the pull.
Slowly let the rope travel back to the start over 2 seconds and repeat for 12 to 20 reps.
mistakes: Pulling the rope toward the chin or chest, which turns the lift into a row.
Letting the elbows drop, swapping rear-delt work for biceps engagement.
Rounding the upper back as you pull, hiding the mid-back contraction.
Loading too heavy and shrugging the traps up, hiding the rear delts under upper-trap dominance.
benefits: Isolates the rear delts in a locked-in seated position.
Reinforces healthy shoulder posture for desk workers and lifters.
Strengthens the small stabilizers around the shoulder blade for joint health.

name: Cable Side Bend
summary: A standing cable side bend that loads the obliques against constant tension for a stronger, more defined waist.
instructions: Set the pulley to the lowest position and attach a single handle, then stand sideways to the cable stack.
Grip the handle with the hand closest to the stack and stand tall with feet hip-width apart.
Place your non-working hand on your hip and let the cable pull you slightly toward the stack at the start.
Bend sideways away from the stack by contracting the obliques on the far side of your body.
Pause at the end of the bend with a hard oblique squeeze, keeping the hips square and chest tall.
Return slowly to the start over 2 seconds, then repeat for 12 to 15 reps before switching sides.
mistakes: Bending forward or backward instead of straight to the side, taking the obliques out of the lift.
Using the arm to pull the cable up, which turns the lift into a one-arm shrug.
Letting the hips shift sideways, which steals load from the obliques.
Rushing the rep and bouncing at the bottom instead of controlling the return phase.
benefits: Builds the obliques with constant cable tension.
Strengthens lateral core control for sport, rotation, and bracing.
Trains each side of the core independently to fix imbalances.

name: Cable Single Arm Neutral Grip Row
summary: A single-arm cable row with a neutral-grip handle that builds the lats and biceps one side at a time.
instructions: Set the cable pulley to chest height and attach a single neutral-grip handle, then grip it with one hand.
Step back until the cable has tension at full arm extension and stand in a staggered stance.
Brace your core and place your non-working hand on your hip or a stable surface for support.
Pull the handle toward your lower ribs, keeping the elbow close to your side and leading with the elbow.
Squeeze your shoulder blade back and down at the end of the pull, feeling the lat engage.
Slowly let the handle travel back to full arm extension over 2 to 3 seconds, then repeat for 10 to 15 reps per side.
mistakes: Rotating the torso to throw the elbow back, which steals load from the lat.
Letting the elbow flare wide, which loads the rear delt instead of the lat.
Shrugging the shoulder up at the end of the pull, swapping lat work for trap engagement.
Snapping the handle back forward and skipping the slow return, where most of the growth lives.
benefits: Builds the lats and biceps one side at a time to fix imbalances.
Trains a joint-friendly neutral grip that protects wrists and shoulders.
Reinforces the horizontal pull pattern that balances pressing work.

name: Cable Single Arm Rear Delt Row
summary: A standing one-arm cable row at shoulder height, pulling a pronated handle out and back to load the rear deltoid.
instructions: Set a D-handle on a cable pulley at about shoulder height.
Stand side-on to the stack, hold the handle in the far hand with a pronated grip, and rest the free hand on the torso.
Step out until the cable is taut and the working arm is straight at shoulder height.
Brace the trunk so the torso does not rotate toward the stack.
Pull the elbow out and back at shoulder height until the hand approaches the chest.
Extend the arm forward under control and repeat, then switch sides.
mistakes: Dropping the elbow below shoulder height, which hands the row to the lats.
Twisting the torso to move the stack instead of rowing with the shoulder.
Using a hammer or supinated grip that changes the rear-delt line.
Shrugging the working shoulder up toward the ear.
benefits: Targets the rear deltoid one arm at a time with constant cable tension.
Lets you match left and right volume when one side lags.
Fits a standard cable tower, so it belongs in cable shoulder collections.

name: Cable Single Arm Rope Pushdown
summary: A one-arm rope pushdown that isolates each triceps independently for a deeper squeeze and better symmetry.
instructions: Set the pulley to the highest position and attach a rope, then grip one end with one hand using a neutral grip.
Step close to the stack and tuck your working elbow tight against your ribs with the forearm parallel to the floor.
Place your non-working hand on your hip and brace your core to keep the torso square to the cable.
Press the rope end straight down by extending the elbow until the arm is fully locked out.
Rotate the palm down at the bottom for an extra triceps squeeze, then pause briefly at lockout.
Let the rope travel back up slowly over 2 seconds and repeat for 10 to 15 reps per side.
mistakes: Letting the elbow flare forward, turning the lift into a chest-driven press.
Twisting the torso to muscle the rope down, which steals load from the triceps.
Cutting the lockout short, missing the strongest contraction at the bottom.
Bouncing the weight up at the top instead of controlling the return.
benefits: Builds triceps size one side at a time to fix imbalances.
Trains a deeper contraction than a two-handed pushdown allows.
Reinforces stable elbow mechanics for stronger pressing lifts.

name: Cable Single Arm Underhand Grip Row
summary: A single-arm cable row with an underhand grip that bias the lats and lower lats with deeper biceps engagement.
instructions: Set the cable pulley to chest height and attach a single handle, then grip it underhand with one hand.
Step back until the cable has tension at full arm extension and stand in a staggered stance.
Brace your core and place your non-working hand on your hip or a stable surface for support.
Pull the handle toward your lower ribs with the elbow tucked tight to your side, palm facing up.
Squeeze the lat hard at the end of the pull, keeping the chest tall and the shoulder packed down.
Slowly let the handle travel back to full arm extension over 2 to 3 seconds, then repeat for 10 to 15 reps per side.
mistakes: Rotating the torso to throw the elbow back, stealing load from the lat.
Letting the elbow flare out wide, which kills the lower-lat focus the underhand grip is meant to create.
Curling the handle toward the shoulder instead of rowing toward the ribs, turning the lift into a biceps curl.
Snapping the handle back forward and skipping the slow return, where most of the growth lives.
benefits: Builds the lats with a stronger lower-lat bias from the underhand grip.
Trains one side at a time to expose and fix imbalances.
Engages the biceps more directly for added pull-day arm work.

name: Cable Single Leg Laying Leg Curl
summary: Prone single leg curl with an ankle cuff on a low cable that isolates one hamstring at a time.
instructions: Attach an ankle cuff to a low pulley and fasten it to one ankle.
Lie face down on a bench set in front of the stack with your knees at the edge.
Extend both legs and grip the bench for stability.
Brace your abs and press your hips into the bench.
Curl the working heel toward your glutes by bending only at the knee.
Pause at the top, lower under control, then finish the set and swap legs.
mistakes: Lifting the hips off the bench, which adds hip flexion and hides a short range.
Letting the cuffed leg drop back down, which throws away the eccentric.
Loading heavy enough to twist the pelvis, so the trunk rotates instead of the knee bending.
Setting the pulley too high, which drags the cuff up the shin and changes the line of pull.
benefits: Trains one hamstring at a time so the stronger leg cannot compensate.
Cable tension stays on the hamstring at full knee flexion.
Useful for spotting and closing side to side strength gaps.

name: Cable Standing Low To High Wood Chopper
summary: A standing low-to-high cable chop that builds rotational power through the obliques and full midsection.
instructions: Set the pulley to the lowest position and attach a single handle, then stand sideways to the cable stack.
Grip the handle with both hands and stand with feet shoulder-width apart, knees slightly bent.
Brace your core and start with the handle near the hip closest to the stack, arms extended.
Rotate your torso and pull the handle up and across your body to overhead on the opposite side.
Pivot the back foot and let the hips follow the rotation, finishing with arms extended overhead.
Reverse the path slowly back to the starting position over 2 to 3 seconds, then repeat for 10 reps per side.
mistakes: Pulling with the arms instead of rotating from the core, which kills the oblique engagement.
Keeping the feet locked flat, which blocks the hips and forces the lower back to take over the rotation.
Rushing the descent and letting the cable yank the handle back instead of controlling the return.
Loading too heavy and rounding the lower back at the top, which risks spinal strain.
benefits: Builds rotational power through the obliques and full midsection.
Trains hip-to-shoulder energy transfer used in throwing and striking sports.
Strengthens the core in a standing, sport-relevant pattern.

name: Cable Standing Single Arm Chest Press
summary: A standing one-arm cable press that trains the chest, front delts, and triceps while exposing side-to-side strength gaps.
instructions: Set the cable pulley to chest height and grip the handle with one hand, palm facing down.
Step forward into a split stance with the working side back, then square your shoulders and hips to the front.
Brace your core hard so the cable can't pull your torso into rotation as you start the press.
Press the handle straight forward until your arm is fully extended, keeping your shoulder pulled back.
Pause for a beat at full extension, feeling the chest and triceps under tension before reversing.
Return the handle slowly to your chest under control, then repeat for reps before switching sides.
mistakes: Letting the torso rotate toward the cable, which dumps the load into the obliques and out of the chest.
Pressing across the body instead of straight forward, shortening the range and reducing chest work.
Standing too close to the stack so the cable goes slack at the start of the rep, killing tension.
Shrugging the shoulder up at full extension instead of keeping the shoulder blade pinned down.
benefits: Builds unilateral chest, front-shoulder, and triceps strength.
Trains core anti-rotation strength under a real pressing load.
Surfaces and corrects left-right pressing imbalances.

name: Cable Supinating Row
summary: A horizontal cable row that rotates the palms up at the finish to load the lats and biceps in the same pull.
instructions: Attach two single-handle attachments to a low cable pulley and grip them with palms facing each other.
Step back until the cables have full tension and stand tall with a slight knee bend and braced trunk.
Pull both handles toward your ribs while rotating your wrists so your palms finish facing up at the top.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the end of the pull, feeling the lats and biceps light up.
Pause briefly with the elbows behind your torso, then begin reversing under control.
Rotate the palms back to neutral as your arms straighten, fighting the cable the whole way out.
mistakes: Skipping the wrist rotation and rowing with a fixed grip, which loses the extra biceps and lat finish.
Leaning back to use bodyweight instead of pulling cleanly with the back muscles.
Letting the elbows drift wide so the rear delts take over and the lats stop working.
Snapping back to the start position and skipping the slow return where most growth tension lives.
benefits: Builds the lats and biceps together with a strong end-range squeeze.
Adds detail and volume to horizontal pulling work in any back program.
Trains the rotated-grip pattern that mirrors chin-up and curl positions.

name: Cable Tricep Kickback
summary: A hinged one-arm cable extension: the upper arm stays beside the torso while the elbow straightens behind the hip.
instructions: Clip a single handle to a low or mid pulley and stand facing the stack.
Hinge the hips, plant the feet, and rest the free hand on the thigh.
Bring the working upper arm beside the torso so it is roughly parallel to the floor, elbow bent about 90 degrees.
Keep that elbow still and extend the forearm backward until the arm is straight.
Squeeze the triceps at lockout without swinging the shoulder.
Bend the elbow under control to return, then repeat and switch arms.
mistakes: Dropping the working elbow, which shortens the range and turns the lift into a curl.
Swinging the whole arm from the shoulder instead of isolating the elbow.
Standing too upright so the cable no longer lines up with the forearm.
Using so much load that the torso has to heave each rep.
benefits: Isolates the triceps at peak contraction with constant cable tension.
Lets you train one arm at a time when a side lags.
Fits a standard cable tower, so it belongs in cable arm collections.

name: Cable Wood Chopper
summary: A diagonal cable rotation that trains the obliques to drive force from a high anchor down across the body.
instructions: Anchor the cable at the highest pulley setting and grip the handle with both hands above one shoulder.
Step out into a wide, athletic stance with feet planted and your knees softly bent.
Brace your core, then pull the handle down and across your body toward the opposite hip.
Drive the rotation with your trunk, letting your back foot pivot naturally as your hips turn.
Pause for a beat at the bottom with arms straight and core locked, feeling the obliques under load.
Return the handle slowly back to the start position above your shoulder, then repeat for reps.
mistakes: Pulling with the arms instead of rotating through the trunk, which removes the obliques from the lift.
Letting the hips stay locked so all the motion happens at the lower back, risking strain.
Using too much weight and yanking the cable, which trades clean rotation for momentum.
Standing too close to the stack so the cable loses tension at the top of every rep.
benefits: Builds rotational power through the obliques and trunk.
Trains the core to transfer force between hips and shoulders.
Carries directly into golf, tennis, throwing, and striking sports.

name: Cable Wrist Curl
summary: Seated cable wrist curl with the forearms braced that isolates wrist flexion and builds grip strength.
instructions: Attach a straight bar to a low pulley and set a light weight.
Sit on a bench facing the stack with your feet about shoulder width apart.
Grip the bar underhand at shoulder width and rest your elbows on your inner thighs.
Let the bar drop by bending only at the wrists, allowing it to roll toward your fingers.
Close your grip and curl your wrists upward, squeezing the forearms at the top.
Pause briefly, then lower under control and repeat for reps.
mistakes: Loading too heavy, which turns the rep into an elbow curl and hides the wrist range.
Lifting the elbows off the thighs, so the forearms move and the wrists stay locked.
Skipping the roll to the fingers, which leaves out the grip closing part of the movement.
Bouncing at the bottom, which loads the wrist joint rather than the flexors.
benefits: Isolates wrist flexion, which most pulling exercises never train directly.
Builds the forearm flexors that close the grip on bars and handles.
Cable tension stays even across a very short range of motion.

name: Calf Press
summary: A plantar flexion press on a horizontal leg press, driving the plate with the balls of the feet only.
instructions: Load the machine and sit with your back flat against the pad.
Place your feet on the plate at shoulder width and extend your legs.
Release the safeties, then slide your feet down so only the balls contact the plate.
Keep the knees just short of lockout and let your heels drop into a full stretch.
Push the plate away by extending the ankles and squeeze at the top.
Lower under control, then re-engage the safeties before stepping out.
mistakes: Bending and straightening the knees, which turns the movement back into a leg press.
Bouncing out of the bottom, which skips the stretched position where the calves work hardest.
Pressing through the toes rather than the ball of the foot, which cramps the forefoot.
Repositioning the feet with the safeties disengaged, which risks the plate dropping.
benefits: Loads the calves heavily without needing a dedicated calf raise machine.
The seat and back pad remove balance, so the ankle can move through full range.
Knee angle can be set to bias the gastrocnemius or the soleus.

name: Captain's Chair Knee Raise
summary: A supported hanging knee raise from a captain's chair station, curling the pelvis to load the abdominals directly.
instructions: Step into a captain's chair station and place your forearms on the pads with your back against the rest.
Grip the handles, let your legs hang straight down and take the weight off your feet.
Brace your abdominals and press your lower back lightly into the pad.
Raise both knees toward your chest, finishing the rep by curling the pelvis upward.
Pause at the top with the abdominals fully shortened.
Lower the legs slowly back to a straight hang and repeat without swinging.
mistakes: Swinging the legs up with momentum, which lets the hip flexors do the work the abdominals should do.
Stopping at hip height without tilting the pelvis, which leaves the rectus abdominis barely loaded.
Dropping the legs at the end of the rep, which throws away the eccentric and stresses the low back.
Shrugging into the shoulder pads, which loads the neck and traps instead of the trunk.
benefits: Ranked first for oblique activation and second for rectus abdominis activation in electromyography testing across thirteen abdominal movements.
Supports the back and forearms, so grip strength does not limit the set the way it does when hanging from a bar.
Progresses simply by moving from bent knees to straight legs without changing the setup.

name: Cat-Camel
summary: A quadruped spinal mobility drill that rounds the back into flexion, then drops it into extension.
instructions: Kneel on the floor with your knees under your hips and your hands under your shoulders.
Set a long, level spine so the back is neither rounded nor sagging.
Exhale and round the whole spine toward the ceiling, tucking the pelvis and dropping the chin.
Hold the rounded position briefly while the arms stay straight and the hands stay planted.
Inhale and reverse: tilt the pelvis forward, let the belly drop, and lift the chest.
Return to the neutral tabletop and repeat the two phases as a slow cycle.
mistakes: Locking the elbows and bouncing the whole trunk as one piece instead of moving vertebra by vertebra.
Forcing the chin to the chest in the rounded phase, which strains the neck.
Collapsing the shoulders toward the ears instead of keeping them stacked over the hands.
Rushing the cycle so the spine never actually flexes or extends through its range.
benefits: Trains controlled spinal flexion and extension in a low-load quadruped position.
Needs no equipment, so it fits warm-ups, cool-downs, and travel programming.
Gives a clear visual of pelvic tilt, which carries into later hinge and brace work.

name: Chest-Supported Dumbbell Row
summary: A prone incline dumbbell row that removes the hinge so the mid back and lats work without lower back load.
instructions: Set an adjustable bench to roughly 45 degrees and pick up two dumbbells.
Lie face down on the pad with your chest supported and your arms hanging.
Hold the dumbbells with palms facing each other and neutral wrists.
Retract your shoulder blades and pull your elbows behind your body.
Stop when your elbows reach or just pass the line of your torso.
Lower the dumbbells slowly to full arm extension and repeat.
mistakes: Peeling the chest off the pad to add range, which reintroduces the back extension you removed.
Swinging the dumbbells up, so the pull comes from momentum rather than muscle.
Shrugging the shoulders toward the ears instead of retracting the blades.
Squeezing the handles hard with a full grip, which lets the biceps take over the pull.
benefits: Rows heavy loads without stressing the lower back.
Chest support removes momentum so each rep stays strict.
Neutral grip is comfortable for shoulders and wrists.

name: Chest-Supported T-Bar Row
summary: A plate-loaded T-bar row taken from a prone chest pad, so the mid back and lats pull without a free hinge.
instructions: Load plates onto the T-bar row post and set the chest pad height.
Lie chest down on the pad with your feet flat on the platform.
Take the handles with a neutral or overhand grip and straighten your arms.
Brace your abdominals and pull your shoulder blades together.
Row the handles back until your elbows pass the line of your torso.
Lower the load under control to a full stretch and repeat.
mistakes: Pushing the chest off the pad to finish the rep, which loads the lumbar spine.
Cutting the range short at the bottom, so the lats never reach full stretch.
Leading with the hands instead of the elbows, which shifts work to the biceps.
Choosing a load that forces jerky partial reps, which trains momentum not the back.
benefits: Strict heavy rowing with no hinge or bracing requirement.
Fixed path keeps the elbow line consistent rep to rep.
Neutral and overhand grips both train the mid back.

name: Chin Ups
summary: A vertical bodyweight pull with palms facing you that builds the lats, biceps, and grip in one of the most honest strength tests there is.
instructions: Reach up and grip the bar with palms facing you, hands about shoulder-width apart.
Hang at full arm extension with the shoulders pulled down away from the ears and the core braced.
Pull yourself up by driving the elbows down toward your ribs, leading with the chest.
Continue the pull until your chin clears the bar and your upper chest is close to the bar.
Pause for a beat at the top, squeezing the back and biceps without swinging.
Lower yourself slowly to a full hang over 2 to 3 seconds, then repeat for reps.
mistakes: Kipping or swinging the legs to generate momentum instead of pulling cleanly with the back and arms.
Cutting the range short by stopping before the chin clears the bar or skipping the full hang at the bottom.
Shrugging the shoulders up at the start so the traps take over and the lats never engage.
Dropping fast at the bottom and skipping the slow lowering phase, where most of the strength gains happen.
benefits: Builds the lats, biceps, and grip with one bodyweight movement.
Develops relative strength that transfers to climbing, sport, and lifting.
Trains the vertical pull pattern that balances out pressing work.

name: Close-Grip Barbell Curl
summary: Standing barbell curl with the hands set inside shoulder width, shifting emphasis toward the outer biceps.
instructions: Load a straight barbell and stand with your feet about hip width apart.
Take an underhand grip with your hands inside shoulder width.
Stand tall with the bar at arms length and your elbows at your sides.
Brace your abs and curl the bar toward your shoulders.
Squeeze the biceps at the top without letting the elbows travel forward.
Lower under control, stopping just short of a locked elbow, then repeat.
mistakes: Swinging the hips to start the bar moving, which takes load off the biceps.
Letting the elbows drift back behind the torso, which shortens the working range.
Gripping so narrow that the wrists ache, which limits load before the biceps are trained.
Dropping the bar quickly, which skips the eccentric where much of the stimulus sits.
benefits: Trains elbow flexion with a fixed grip width that is easy to repeat session to session.
The narrow grip shifts emphasis toward the outer part of the biceps.
A bar allows small load jumps, so progression is simple to track.

name: Close-Grip Push-Up off a Dumbbell
summary: A close-grip push-up with both hands stacked on a single upright dumbbell under the chest.
instructions: Stand one dumbbell on its end on the floor under your chest.
Place both hands on the top head, side by side, and step back into a high plank.
Brace the trunk so the body is a straight line from head to heels.
Lower the chest toward the dumbbell with the elbows tracking close to the ribs.
Stop just short of the top head, then press back to straight elbows.
Keep the dumbbell still; if it rocks, reset your hands and the plank before the next rep.
mistakes: Flaring the elbows, which turns a close-grip press into a standard push-up.
Letting the dumbbell rock, which dumps the wrists and the shoulder.
Piking or sagging the hips, which breaks the plank the chest is supposed to press from.
Locking the elbows hard at the top, which dumps tension off the triceps.
benefits: The narrow hand set loads the triceps more than a shoulder-width floor push-up.
One dumbbell is enough kit for a close-grip press at home.
The raised head gives a little extra chest travel without a pair of push-up handles.

name: Controlled Forearm Pronation and Supination
summary: A standing single-dumbbell drill that rotates the forearm from palm-up to palm-down with the elbow fixed.
instructions: Stand tall with a light dumbbell in one hand and the opposite arm relaxed at your side.
Pin the working upper arm to the torso and bend the elbow to about 90 degrees.
Hold the handle at its center with the wrist straight and the thumb pointing up.
Rotate the forearm until the palm faces down, keeping the elbow glued to the waist.
Reverse the rotation until the palm faces up, still without moving the upper arm.
Finish the set, then switch hands and repeat.
mistakes: Letting the elbow drift forward, which turns the drill into a curl.
Bending or extending the wrist, which loads the flexors instead of the rotators.
Using a heavy dumbbell that forces the shoulder to swing the weight around.
Snapping through the end ranges instead of slowing the last third of each turn.
benefits: Trains the forearm rotators that gripping, throwing, and racquet work actually use.
A light dumbbell and a fixed elbow make the drill usable in rehab-adjacent programming.
Unilateral loading shows side-to-side differences without a cable stack.

name: Copenhagen Plank
summary: Bench-supported side plank that loads the inner thighs while the trunk holds a straight, stable position.
instructions: Lie on your side beside a stable bench and place your top ankle on its pad.
Position your supporting elbow below your shoulder and rest the forearm on the floor.
Press the upper ankle into the bench as you lift your hips.
Bring the lower leg up beneath the bench while keeping your torso side-on.
Hold a straight line from the supporting shoulder through the hips to the upper ankle.
Lower the hips under control and reset before repeating on the other side.
mistakes: Letting the pelvis sag during the raised hold.
Rolling the chest toward the floor.
Allowing the top ankle to slide off its support.
Rushing the hip lift and descent.
benefits: Loads the hip adductors directly.
Challenges abdominal control in a side-plank position.
Provides a bench-supported option for adductor training.

name: Cossack Squat
summary: A deep sideways squat on one leg with the other leg extended straight, worked in the frontal plane.
instructions: Stand with your feet well outside shoulder width and toes pointing forward.
Brace your abdominals and lift your chest tall.
Shift your weight over one leg and bend that knee, sitting the hips back and down.
Keep the other leg straight and let its foot roll onto the heel with the toes up.
Descend only as far as your hips and ankles allow with the loaded heel flat.
Push through the bent leg to return to center, then repeat on the other side.
mistakes: Arching the lower back to reach depth, which loads the lumbar spine instead of the hips.
Letting the heel of the squatting leg lift, which is an ankle mobility limit, not a strength one.
Bending the extended leg, which removes the adductor and hamstring stretch.
Rushing the transition between sides, which loses control at the deepest position.
benefits: Trains strength in the frontal plane that forward facing leg work misses.
Loads the adductors and hamstrings of the extended leg through a long stretch.
Builds hip, knee and ankle range that carries over to every squat pattern.

name: Cross-Body Cable Tricep Extension
summary: A high-pulley triceps extension that drives the working arm across the body from the opposite shoulder to lockout.
instructions: Set a cable at a high pulley and hold the bare cable end in the working hand.
Stand beside the stack and bring that hand to the opposite shoulder, elbow bent.
Rest the free hand behind your back and brace the trunk so the torso stays still.
Keep the working upper arm fixed and extend the elbow until the arm is straight.
Pause at lockout, then bend the elbow under control back to the opposite shoulder.
Finish the set, then switch arms.
mistakes: Letting the elbow drift forward, which turns an isolation into a shoulder press-down.
Leaning the torso into the cable, which hides how little the triceps moved.
Snapping the lockout, which dumps tension at the only part of the range that matters here.
Using a D-handle the approved clip does not show, which changes the grip and the line of pull.
benefits: Constant cable tension keeps the triceps loaded through the whole elbow range.
The cross-body path shortens the long head at lockout, which a straight pushdown does less of.
Training one arm at a time makes left-to-right differences obvious.

name: Cross-Body Hammer Curl
summary: Dumbbell hammer curl swept diagonally across the torso, loading the biceps, brachialis and forearms.
instructions: Hold a dumbbell in each hand at your sides with your palms facing your body.
Stand tall with your feet hip width apart and your abs braced.
Keep a small bend in the elbows and set your shoulders back and down.
Curl one dumbbell diagonally across your chest toward the opposite shoulder.
Squeeze at the top without letting the dumbbell touch your body.
Lower under control to your side, then repeat with the other arm.
mistakes: Resting the dumbbell against the chest at the top, which unloads the arm mid rep.
Rotating the torso to meet the dumbbell, which shortens the range the arm actually works.
Letting the elbow swing forward, so the front of the shoulder lifts the weight.
Shrugging the shoulder up as the dumbbell rises, which moves work to the traps.
benefits: Neutral grip loads the brachialis and brachioradialis alongside the biceps.
One arm at a time makes side to side rep and load matching simple.
Needs only a pair of dumbbells, so it fits home and hotel gym programs.

name: Crunches
summary: A short-range supine trunk curl that lifts the shoulder blades while the lower back stays on the floor.
instructions: Lie on your back with your knees bent and your feet flat, heels about a foot from your hips.
Place your hands behind your head with the elbows open, or cross the arms on the chest.
Press the lower back gently into the floor and brace the abdominals.
Exhale and curl the rib cage toward the pelvis until the shoulder blades lift off the mat.
Pause with the lumbar spine still in contact with the floor.
Inhale and lower under control without dropping the head between reps.
mistakes: Yanking on the head with the hands, which strains the neck and fakes trunk range.
Curling all the way to a sit-up, which hands the work to the hip flexors.
Lifting the lower back off the floor, which turns a short curl into a swing.
Racing the reps so the abdominals never stay shortened at the top.
benefits: Isolates the abdominals through a short range with the lumbar spine supported.
Needs no equipment, so it fits any room, travel context, or beginner block.
Serves as the reference trunk-flexion clip that decline and weighted variants are compared against.

name: Cuban Press
summary: A three-phase dumbbell drill that links an upright row, an external rotation and an overhead press in one rep.
instructions: Stand tall with a light dumbbell in each hand, palms facing your thighs.
Set your shoulder blades down and back and brace your trunk.
Pull the dumbbells up the front of your body until the upper arms are parallel to the floor.
Holding the elbows at that height, rotate the forearms up and back into a goalpost position.
Press the dumbbells overhead until the arms are almost straight.
Reverse the three phases in order and return to the start under control.
mistakes: Loading it like a shoulder press, which makes the rotation phase impossible to control.
Letting the elbows drop during the rotation, which removes the external rotation the exercise exists for.
Arching the lower back to finish the press, which hides limited overhead mobility.
Rushing the sequence, which blends the three phases and loses the cuff work entirely.
benefits: Loads the rotator cuff in a rotated overhead position that most pressing movements do not reach.
Combines mobility and strength work in a single rep, which saves warm-up time.
Exposes shoulder mobility restrictions early, before heavier pressing is loaded.

name: Cycling Cooldown
summary: Seated bicycle pedalling shown as a cycling cooldown, with the hands on the handlebars and the legs moving through continuous pedal strokes.
instructions: Sit on the bicycle saddle with both feet positioned on the pedals.
Place both hands on the handlebars and settle into a steady riding posture.
Continue pedalling smoothly while remaining seated.
Reduce the workload gradually toward an easy effort.
Keep the shoulders relaxed and avoid excessive side-to-side rocking.
Follow the cooldown duration specified for the cycling session.
mistakes: Maintaining the hard work interval throughout the cooldown.
Rocking the hips from side to side while pedalling.
Gripping the handlebars with unnecessarily tense shoulders.
Using a gear that makes the pedal stroke uneven.
benefits: Demonstrates the seated pedalling pattern used in cycling.
Provides an on-bike movement for the end of a cycling session.
Shows coordinated lower-body movement through repeated pedal strokes.

name: Cycling Intervals
summary: Seated cycling run as repeated hard efforts with recoveries between them, holding a stable position throughout.
instructions: Set saddle height so your knee stays slightly bent at the bottom of the stroke.
Ride easy for several minutes until your breathing and cadence settle.
Hold a stable seated position with relaxed shoulders and a light grip.
Lift effort to the target for the work interval without changing your position.
Drop back to easy pedalling for the full recovery before the next effort.
Repeat the work and recovery pattern, then ride easy to finish.
mistakes: Starting the first effort too hard, so the last intervals collapse.
Cutting recovery short, which turns the session into one long moderate ride.
Rocking the hips at high effort instead of driving through the pedals.
Raising cadence without resistance, so effort never reaches the target.
benefits: Improves ventilatory threshold within a small number of sessions.
Keeps a low-impact pattern while intensity climbs.
Uses a repeatable structure that is easy to prescribe and track.

name: Cycling Sprint
summary: Maximal short cycling efforts where output peaks in seconds and the quads carry the load through every pedal stroke.
instructions: Warm up with several minutes of easy riding before attempting any sprint.
Select a resistance heavy enough that cadence cannot run away from you.
Settle into a stable seated position with a firm grip on the bars.
Accelerate to maximum effort within the first few pedal strokes.
Hold peak output for the full sprint window without shifting position.
Spin easy for several minutes of recovery before the next sprint.
mistakes: Sprinting against too little resistance, so cadence spikes and force stays low.
Building up gradually, which wastes most of a thirty-second window.
Shortening recovery, which caps the output of every subsequent sprint.
Sprinting cold, which is when hamstring and knee complaints appear.
benefits: Raises ventilatory threshold in as few as six sessions.
Delivers maximal intensity without impact on the joints.
Produces a clean, measurable output for testing and pacing.

name: Cycling Warmup
summary: Seated bicycle pedalling shown as a cycling warm-up, with the hands on the handlebars and the legs moving through continuous pedal strokes.
instructions: Sit on the bicycle saddle with both feet positioned on the pedals.
Place both hands on the handlebars and settle into a steady riding posture.
Begin pedalling smoothly while remaining seated.
Start with an easy effort before increasing the workload gradually.
Keep the shoulders relaxed and avoid excessive side-to-side rocking.
Follow the warm-up progression specified for the cycling session.
mistakes: Beginning with a hard effort before easing into the ride.
Rocking the hips from side to side while pedalling.
Gripping the handlebars with unnecessarily tense shoulders.
Using a gear that makes the pedal stroke uneven.
benefits: Demonstrates the seated pedalling pattern used in cycling.
Provides a cycling-specific opening movement for a warm-up sequence.
Shows coordinated lower-body movement through repeated pedal strokes.

name: Dead Bug
summary: A supine anti-extension core drill that lowers one arm and the opposite leg while the lower back stays pinned down.
instructions: Lie on your back on a mat with your arms reaching straight toward the ceiling.
Lift your feet so your hips and knees are both bent to ninety degrees.
Press your lower back gently into the floor and brace your abdominals.
Exhale and lower one arm overhead while extending the opposite leg toward the floor.
Stop just short of the floor while the lower back stays flat, then inhale and return.
Repeat with the opposite arm and leg, alternating for the prescribed reps.
mistakes: Letting the lower back arch off the floor, which means the core has stopped resisting extension.
Moving faster than you can breathe, which turns a control drill into a flailing exercise.
Reaching further than you can hold position, which trades range for the stability being trained.
Holding the breath throughout, which reduces the bracing the movement is meant to teach.
benefits: Trains anti-extension core control in a position that keeps load off the spine.
Needs nothing but a mat, so it fits home, travel and rehab adjacent programming.
Scales in both directions by changing limb range or adding light external load.

name: Dead Bug (Weighted)
summary: A loaded dead bug that holds two dumbbells overhead while opposite limbs extend with the low back pinned.
instructions: Lie on your back holding a light dumbbell in each hand, arms straight toward the ceiling.
Lift both feet so the hips and knees are bent to 90 degrees and the shins are level.
Press the lower back into the floor and brace the abdominals.
Exhale and lower one dumbbell overhead while extending the opposite leg toward the floor.
Stop just short of the floor while the lumbar spine stays flat, then return both limbs.
Repeat on the other diagonal, keeping both feet off the ground between reps.
mistakes: Letting the lower back arch off the floor, which means the core has stopped resisting extension.
Planting the feet, which turns a tabletop dead bug into a crook-lying sit-up setup.
Reaching farther than you can hold position, which trades range for the stability being trained.
Choosing dumbbells so heavy that the ribs flare before the first rep finishes.
benefits: Adds anti-extension load without taking the drill off the floor.
The contralateral pattern still trains coordination while the weights raise the demand.
Scales from a bodyweight dead bug with the same camera and the same lumbar cue.

name: Dead Hang
summary: An isometric hang from an overhead bar that loads the grip and forearm flexors while the upper body decompresses.
instructions: Set a bench or box under a secure pull-up bar so you can reach it without jumping.
Take an overhand grip slightly wider than shoulder width with the thumbs wrapped around the bar.
Step off the support and let your body hang with the arms straight.
Keep the neck long and let the shoulders relax toward the ears in a passive hang.
Squeeze the glutes lightly and hold the legs still so the body does not swing.
Hold for the prescribed time, then step back onto the support before releasing the bar.
mistakes: Jumping to the bar and dropping off it, which loads cold shoulders and wrists at speed.
Gripping without wrapping the thumb, which ends the hang well before the forearms are trained.
Holding the arms slightly bent, which fatigues the biceps and hides the grip work.
Letting the body swing, which spreads the load unevenly across the shoulders.
benefits: Builds grip and forearm endurance that carries into deadlifts, rows and pull-ups.
Lengthens the shoulders and upper back under bodyweight without any active effort.
Requires only a bar, and progress is measured in seconds rather than reps.

name: Decline Barbell Bench Press
summary: Barbell press performed head-down on a decline bench, driving from just below the sternum to full extension.
instructions: Set a decline bench, load the bar, and hook your feet securely under the leg pad.
Lie back with your eyes under the bar and grip it just outside shoulder width.
Pinch your shoulder blades together and drive them into the pad, then take the lift-off with a spotter.
Inhale and lower the bar in a straight line to the base of your sternum until it touches your chest.
Press the bar back up by driving your upper back into the bench and extending your elbows.
Stop just short of full lockout to keep tension, then repeat for the prescribed reps.
mistakes: Bouncing the bar off the chest replaces muscular work with momentum and puts a shock load on the shoulders.
Letting the shoulder blades come unset during the press hands the load to the front of the shoulder joint.
Unracking a heavy bar without a spotter in the decline position leaves no safe way out of a failed rep.
Letting the wrists roll back into extension puts the bar behind the forearm and strains the wrist joint.
benefits: Shortens the pressing range compared with a flat bench, which some lifters tolerate better at the shoulder.
Keeps triceps involvement high, so it doubles as elbow extension volume on a chest day.
Completes the bench-angle set, giving a third loading position for the pectorals.

name: Decline Crunch
summary: A partial-range trunk curl on a decline bench that keeps the lower back down and loads the abdominals against gravity.
instructions: Set a decline bench to a moderate angle and hook your feet under the roller pads.
Lie back with your knees bent and your lower back resting on the bench.
Cross your arms over your chest or rest your fingertips beside your ears without pulling on the neck.
Exhale and curl your shoulder blades off the bench by shortening the abdominals.
Stop once the upper back has left the pad, keeping the lower back in contact.
Inhale and lower slowly to the start without resting at the bottom.
mistakes: Pulling on the head with the hands, which strains the neck and hides how little the abdominals moved.
Curling all the way up into a sit-up, which hands the work to the hip flexors.
Setting the decline too steep too soon, which usually turns into a swinging half rep.
Dropping back to the bench between reps, which discards the eccentric and the tension with it.
benefits: Increases abdominal loading over a floor crunch without adding any external weight.
Keeps the range short and the lower back supported, which suits high rep finisher work.
Progresses by bench angle alone, so one station covers several difficulty levels.

name: Decline Machine Chest Press
summary: Seated machine press on a downward path that loads the lower chest without a decline bench or a spotter.
instructions: Set the seat height so the handles line up with your lower chest and load the machine.
Sit back with your whole spine against the pad and fasten the seat belt if the machine has one.
Take a handle in each hand with an overhand grip and set your shoulder blades back and down.
Press the handles down and away from your chest until your elbows are almost straight.
Stop just short of locking out and hold the chest contraction briefly.
Return the handles slowly until you feel a stretch across the chest, then repeat.
mistakes: Setting the seat too high turns the movement into a flat or incline press and removes the downward angle.
Letting the shoulders roll forward off the pad at the finish transfers load onto the shoulder joint.
Slamming into full lockout hands the work to the joints and drops tension off the chest.
Letting the stack pull the handles back quickly wastes the eccentric and risks a jolt at the shoulder.
benefits: Delivers a decline pressing angle without an inverted setup or a spotter.
Fixed path lets a beginner load the chest heavily with minimal balance demand.
Independent handles on iso-lateral machines let each side work through its own range.

name: Decline Push Up
summary: A push up with feet elevated on a bench or step that biases the upper chest, front delts, and triceps without any equipment.
instructions: Place your feet on a sturdy bench, step, or low platform and lower your hands to the floor.
Set your hands slightly wider than shoulder width with arms straight and your body in a long line.
Brace your core and squeeze your glutes so your hips don't sag or pike during the rep.
Lower your chest toward the floor under control, keeping the elbows tracked at about 45 degrees.
Pause briefly when your chest is just above the floor, holding tension through the upper body.
Press back up to full arm extension by driving through the chest and triceps, then repeat.
mistakes: Letting the hips sag toward the floor, which kills the line and shifts strain into the lower back.
Flaring the elbows out to 90 degrees, which strains the front shoulders and reduces chest work.
Bouncing at the bottom instead of pausing briefly to control the lift through the full range.
Cutting the range short by stopping a long way above the floor and skipping the deep stretch.
benefits: Biases the upper chest and front shoulders without barbell incline work.
Builds bodyweight pressing strength using only a step or bench.
Bridges the gap between standard push ups and harder pressing variations.

name: Decline Sit-Up
summary: A full-range sit-up on a decline bench, bringing the chest toward the thighs against a steeper gravity angle.
instructions: Set a decline bench and secure both feet under the padded roller.
Lie back with your knees bent and your arms crossed over your chest.
Tuck your chin lightly toward your chest to protect the neck.
Exhale and curl your torso up until your chest travels toward your thighs.
Pause briefly at the top with the abdominals fully shortened.
Lower yourself back to the bench under control and repeat.
mistakes: Yanking on the head or neck to start the rep, which strains the cervical spine.
Letting the hip flexors pull the torso up first, which leaves the abdominals barely loaded.
Dropping back onto the bench at speed, which discards the eccentric and jars the spine.
Choosing a steep decline before the movement is controlled, which forces momentum-driven reps.
benefits: Trains the full trunk flexion range with more resistance than a floor sit-up.
Adjusts difficulty by bench angle, so one station serves several ability levels.
Loads easily with a plate or dumbbell held across the chest when bodyweight stops challenging.

name: Deficit Deadlift
summary: A conventional deadlift pulled while standing on a raised platform, adding range at the bottom of the lift.
instructions: Stand on a stable platform roughly four to eight inches high with the bar over your midfoot.
Set your feet hip width apart and grip the bar just outside your shins.
Drop your hips until your shoulders sit over the bar with the shins near vertical.
Brace your abdominals hard and pull the slack out of the bar.
Drive through the whole foot and extend the hips and knees together to lockout.
Lower the bar under control back to the platform and reset before the next rep.
mistakes: Rounding the lower back to reach the bar, which the added range makes far more likely.
Letting the bar drift forward off the midfoot, which lengthens the lever on the spine.
Standing on a platform that is too high for your current hip and ankle range.
Keeping the same load as a floor pull, which forces the hips to shoot up first.
benefits: Adds range at the hardest part of the pull to build strength off the floor.
Increases the leg drive demand compared with a deadlift from the floor.
May improve the hamstring to quadriceps strength balance.

name: Deficit Dumbbell Romanian Deadlift
summary: A dumbbell Romanian deadlift performed from a raised platform so the hamstrings work through a longer range.
instructions: Stand on a low stable platform with your feet hip width apart.
Hold a dumbbell in each hand at your sides with a neutral grip.
Set your shoulders back and down and brace your abdominals.
Push your hips backward and lower the dumbbells past the edge of the platform.
Stop when the hamstrings reach the end of their stretch with the back still flat.
Drive your hips forward to stand, stopping just short of full extension.
mistakes: Chasing depth past your available range, which rounds the lower back.
Bending the knees further as you descend, which turns the hinge into a squat.
Letting the dumbbells swing away from the legs, which strains the lower back.
Using a platform so high that the heels have nowhere to settle at the bottom.
benefits: Extends the eccentric range of the hinge without adding load.
Keeps continuous tension on the hamstrings and glutes across the set.
Uses dumbbells, so it scales in small steps and needs no rack.

name: Diamond Push Ups
summary: A close-hand push up where the thumbs and index fingers form a diamond — turning a chest move into a triceps builder.
instructions: Get into a high plank with your hands directly under your chest, thumbs and index fingers touching.
Set your feet about hip-width apart and lock your body into a long line from head to heels.
Brace your core and squeeze the glutes so the hips stay in line throughout the rep.
Lower your chest toward your hands while keeping the elbows tucked close to your ribs.
Pause briefly when the chest is just above your hands, feeling the triceps fully loaded.
Press back up to full arm extension by driving through the triceps, then repeat for reps.
mistakes: Flaring the elbows out wide, which turns the lift back into a chest push up and removes the triceps focus.
Letting the hips sag or pike, which breaks the plank line and shifts strain into the lower back.
Not bringing the hands close enough so the diamond shape disappears and the lift loses its triceps bias.
Cutting the range short by stopping high above the hands instead of touching down for full triceps stretch.
benefits: Builds triceps size and strength with only bodyweight.
Develops a stronger lockout that carries into pressing lifts.
Trains a tight, elbow-tucked press pattern that protects the shoulders.

name: Dumbbell Alternating Forward Lunge
summary: A loaded forward lunge that alternates legs each rep — training the quads, glutes, and balance one side at a time.
instructions: Hold a dumbbell in each hand at your sides with arms relaxed and shoulders pulled down and back.
Stand tall with your feet hip-width apart and brace your core to set a stable starting position.
