Dropping the arms at the end of the rep, which throws away the lowering phase.
benefits: The fixed path removes balance and swing, so the side of the deltoid does the work.
Easy to load in small steps, which makes progression simple for beginners.
Seated support means trunk fatigue does not end the set early.

name: Machine Leg Extension
summary: A seated knee-extension machine that isolates the quads through a fixed range — the most direct quad-builder in the gym.
instructions: Sit on the machine and adjust the back pad so your knees line up with the machine's pivot point.
Place your shins behind the roller pad with the pad sitting just above the ankle joint, not on the foot.
Grip the side handles, brace your core, and press your back firmly into the pad.
Extend your knees smoothly until the legs are straight, squeezing the quads hard at the top.
Hold the lockout for a beat, keeping the toes pulled up toward the shins for max quad engagement.
Lower the pad slowly over 2 to 3 seconds back to the start, never letting the stack slam down.
mistakes: Slamming the legs straight with momentum, then dropping the weight fast, which removes most of the loading.
Setting the seat wrong so the knee pivot doesn't match the machine, which puts shear stress on the joint.
Lifting the hips off the seat to muscle the weight up, which shifts work away from the quads.
Cutting the range short on the bottom half, which trains only the easy top portion of the lift.
benefits: Builds quad size with the most direct knee-extension stimulus in the gym.
Isolates the quads cleanly without recruiting the glutes or hamstrings.
Allows safe, scalable loading for both beginners and advanced lifters.

name: Machine Leg Press
summary: A seated leg press that loads the quads and glutes through a guided press — the heavy-load alternative to the back squat.
instructions: Sit in the machine with your back fully against the pad and feet shoulder-width on the platform.
Release the safety handles and grip the side bars to keep your torso and hips locked in place.
Lower the platform slowly toward your chest over 2 to 3 seconds until your knees reach about 90 degrees.
Keep your lower back flat against the pad and your knees tracking in line with your toes.
Drive the platform back up by pressing through the heels and the middle of the foot.
Stop just short of locking the knees at the top, then control the next rep down without resting the stack.
mistakes: Letting the lower back round and lift off the pad at the bottom, which puts the spine at risk.
Locking the knees out hard at the top of every rep, slamming the joint under heavy load.
Letting the knees cave inward on the press, which strains the knees and loses force production.
Cutting the range short and pressing only the top few inches, which trains a fraction of the leg.
benefits: Builds quad and glute strength with heavy, scalable load.
Removes spinal compression while still loading the legs hard.
Provides a safe leg-day option for lifters returning from back issues.

name: Machine Neutral Row
summary: A chest-supported neutral-grip row that trains the lats and mid-back through a fixed horizontal pull — easy to learn, hard to cheat.
instructions: Set the chest pad so it sits across your upper chest with your shoulders just above the handle position.
Grip both neutral handles with palms facing each other and let your arms hang fully extended.
Brace your core and press your chest firmly into the pad to lock your torso in place.
Pull the handles toward your ribs by driving the elbows back and squeezing the shoulder blades together.
Pause at the top of the pull with the elbows behind the body, feeling the mid-back contract hard.
Lower the handles slowly over 2 to 3 seconds back to a full stretch, then repeat without losing chest contact.
mistakes: Pulling with the biceps instead of leading with the elbows, which steals work from the back.
Letting the chest peel off the pad to use body english, which defeats the support and overloads the low back.
Cutting the lowering short and dropping the handles fast, missing most of the muscle-building tension.
Shrugging the shoulders up at the top of the row, swapping mid-back work for trap dominance.
benefits: Builds the lats and mid-back with no lower-back fatigue.
Wrist- and shoulder-friendly thanks to the neutral grip position.
Easy to load progressively without compromising form.

name: Machine Pec Fly
summary: A seated chest fly machine that isolates the pecs through an arc of motion — the cleanest chest-only stimulus in the gym.
instructions: Adjust the seat so the handles sit at chest height with your elbows roughly in line with your shoulders.
Grip both handles with a slight bend in the elbows and press your back firmly into the pad.
Brace your core and pull your shoulder blades back and down to set a stable chest position.
Sweep the handles together in a wide arc by squeezing the chest, keeping the elbow angle fixed.
Pause at the middle when the handles meet, holding a hard chest squeeze for a full beat.
Let the handles open back out slowly over 2 to 3 seconds until you feel a controlled chest stretch.
mistakes: Bending the elbows mid-rep so the lift becomes a press, which removes the chest isolation.
Letting the shoulders roll forward at the stretch position, which strains the front shoulders.
Slamming the handles together with momentum instead of squeezing through the contraction.
Cutting the stretch short and never letting the arms open fully, which trains a tiny portion of the lift.
benefits: Isolates the chest more directly than any pressing movement.
Builds chest size with low joint stress and high mind-muscle feedback.
Easy to load progressively without shoulder or wrist strain.

name: Machine Plate Loaded Front Military Press
summary: A plate-loaded seated press that trains the front delts through a fixed overhead path — a stable alternative to the standing barbell press.
instructions: Set the seat so the handles sit just above shoulder height when your arms are bent and ready to press.
Grip both handles with palms facing forward and press your back firmly into the pad.
Brace your core and press the handles straight up overhead, exhaling as you drive.
Lock out softly at the top with the arms extended, keeping the shoulders down away from the ears.
Lower the handles slowly over 2 to 3 seconds until they return to shoulder level.
Reset the breath and repeat for 8 to 12 reps, keeping the chest proud the whole set.
mistakes: Arching the lower back hard off the pad to use the chest, which strains the spine and loses the shoulder focus.
Letting the handles drift forward instead of pressing straight up, which puts unnecessary load on the front shoulders.
Locking the elbows out hard at the top, slamming the joint instead of stopping with control.
Letting the weight drop fast on the way down and skipping the slow lowering portion of every rep.
benefits: Builds front-shoulder strength and size with reduced balance demand.
Offers a safer overhead pressing option for lifters with low-back issues.
Allows heavier pressing volume thanks to the fixed bar path.

name: Machine Plate Loaded Leg Extension
summary: A plate-loaded seated leg extension that isolates the quads — the heavier-feeling, gym-staple cousin of the selectorized version.
instructions: Sit in the machine and align your knees with the machine's pivot point by adjusting the back pad.
Hook your shins behind the roller pad with the pad just above the ankle joint, not on the foot.
Grip the side handles, brace your core, and press your back firmly into the seat.
Extend the knees smoothly until the legs are straight, driving the lever arm up with the quads.
Squeeze hard at the top with toes pulled toward the shins, holding the contraction for a beat.
Lower the lever slowly over 2 to 3 seconds back to the start, keeping tension on the quads throughout.
mistakes: Loading too many plates and dropping the lever fast, which trains momentum instead of the quads.
Cutting the range short on either end, which trains only the easy middle of the motion.
Lifting the hips off the seat to muscle the lever up, shifting work away from the target.
Hyperextending the knees at the top under heavy load, slamming the joint instead of stopping clean.
benefits: Allows heavier quad isolation than most selectorized stacks.
Builds quad mass with direct, single-joint loading.
Easy to micro-load with small plates for progressive overload.

name: Machine Plate Loaded T Bar Row
summary: A plate-loaded T-bar row that builds the lats and mid-back through a heavy hip-hinge pull — the gym's classic mass-builder.
instructions: Load plates onto the T-bar's loading sleeve and step astride the bar with feet shoulder-width apart.
Hinge at the hips with a flat back and a slight knee bend until you can grip the handles.
Brace your core hard and squeeze your shoulder blades back and down to lock the torso position.
Pull the bar up toward your lower chest by driving the elbows back, leading with the upper back.
Pause briefly at the top of the pull, squeezing the lats and mid-back hard before reversing.
Lower the bar slowly over 2 to 3 seconds back to the start, keeping the hinge position locked the whole rep.
mistakes: Rounding the lower back to lift heavier, which puts serious risk on the spine.
Standing too upright and turning the lift into a shrug instead of a row.
Yanking the bar with body english instead of pulling cleanly with the back.
Cutting the lowering short and letting the bar drop, missing the muscle-building portion of every rep.
benefits: Builds serious lat and mid-back mass with heavy free-weight loading.
Trains the hinge-and-row pattern that carries over to deadlifts.
Allows real progressive overload week over week.

name: Machine Preacher Curl
summary: Seated preacher curl machine that fixes the upper arms on a pad so the biceps work through a strict range.
instructions: Set the seat height so your armpits rest against the top of the pad.
Sit with your chest against the support and your feet flat on the floor.
Take the handles with an underhand grip and lay your upper arms flat on the pad.
Straighten your arms to the start position without fully locking the elbows.
Curl the handles toward your shoulders and squeeze at the top.
Lower under control back to the stretched position and repeat.
mistakes: Sliding the elbows up the pad, which shortens the range the biceps actually work.
Lifting the chest off the support to start the rep, which brings the back into an arm exercise.
Snapping the arms straight at the bottom, which loads the elbow in a stretched position.
Setting the seat too low, so the shoulders shrug up and the pad digs into the arms.
benefits: The pad removes momentum, so the biceps take the load at every rep speed.
A fixed path is quick to teach and easy to load in small steps.
Supported arms let you train close to failure without the torso compensating.

name: Machine Pulldown
summary: A seated machine pulldown that trains the lats and biceps through a fixed vertical pull — the universal gym back-builder.
instructions: Sit on the machine and lock your thighs under the pad with feet flat on the floor.
Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder width with palms facing forward.
Lean your torso back about 10 to 15 degrees and pull your shoulder blades down to set the lats.
Pull the bar down to the upper chest by driving the elbows down and back, not by yanking with the arms.
Pause briefly at the bottom with the bar at your collarbones, squeezing the lats hard.
Let the bar travel slowly back up over 2 to 3 seconds until your arms are fully extended overhead.
mistakes: Pulling with the biceps and forearms instead of leading with the elbows and back.
Leaning too far back so the lift turns into a row instead of a vertical pull.
Cutting the top range short and never letting the arms fully extend, which removes the lat stretch.
Letting the stack snap back up at the top, killing the slow return where most muscle growth happens.
benefits: Builds lat width and back thickness with a beginner-friendly pattern.
Strengthens the vertical pull that transfers directly to pull-ups.
Trains the lats and biceps through a clean, full range of motion.

name: Machine Seated Cable Row
summary: A seated cable row that trains the lats, mid-back, and biceps through a clean horizontal pull — the benchmark row in any gym.
instructions: Sit on the machine and brace your feet against the platform with your knees slightly bent.
Grip the handle, hinge slightly forward, and let the cable pull your arms fully extended.
Sit tall with a flat back and pull your shoulder blades down and back to set the start position.
Pull the handle to your lower chest or upper stomach by driving the elbows back behind the body.
Squeeze the mid-back hard at the top of the pull, pausing for a full beat before reversing.
Let the handle travel slowly back forward over 2 to 3 seconds, fighting the cable the whole way.
mistakes: Rocking the torso back and forth to use momentum, which trains the low back instead of the upper back.
Pulling the handle to the throat instead of the lower chest, which loses the lat engagement.
Shrugging the shoulders up at the top, swapping mid-back work for trap dominance.
Letting the cable rip the arms forward fast and skipping the slow return portion of every rep.
benefits: Builds the lats, mid-back, and biceps with constant cable tension.
Improves posture by training the muscles that pull the shoulders back.
Easy to scale for beginners and easy to load for advanced lifters.

name: Machine Tricep Extension
summary: Seated machine triceps extension that drives the handles forward on a fixed path with the arms supported.
instructions: Adjust the seat so your upper arms rest flat on the pad and your shoulders stay down.
Sit with your back against the support and your feet flat on the floor.
Take the handles with a neutral grip and start with the elbows bent.
Brace your abs so the lower back stays against the pad.
Exhale and extend your elbows to push the handles forward.
Stop just short of lockout, then return the handles slowly and repeat.
mistakes: Locking the elbows hard at the end of each rep, which shifts load onto the joint.
Arching the lower back to press the handles, which recruits the trunk instead of the arms.
Letting the upper arms lift off the pad, so the shoulders help the triceps.
Turning the head to watch the stack, which puts the neck in a loaded rotated position.
benefits: The fixed path means the triceps can be loaded with no balance demand at all.
Simple to teach and quick to adjust between users in a circuit.
Supports pressing strength by training elbow extension directly.

name: Machine Underhand Row
summary: A machine row with an underhand grip that hits the lower lats and biceps hard — the supinated take on the chest-supported row.
instructions: Set the chest pad height so it sits across your upper chest with your shoulders just above the handles.
Grip the underhand handles with palms facing up and let your arms extend fully toward the floor.
Brace your core and press your chest firmly into the pad to lock the torso in place.
Pull the handles up toward your lower ribs by driving the elbows back and down close to the body.
Pause at the top with the elbows behind you, squeezing the lats and biceps for a full beat.
Lower the handles slowly over 2 to 3 seconds back to a full stretch before the next rep.
mistakes: Curling the arms up with the biceps instead of rowing with the elbows leading the motion.
Letting the chest peel off the pad to cheat the weight up, which loads the low back.
Flaring the elbows wide and turning the row into an overhand-style pull, losing the underhand bias.
Cutting the stretch short and never letting the arms fully extend at the bottom of each rep.
benefits: Builds the lower lats with a strong, biceps-friendly pulling line.
Removes lower-back fatigue thanks to the chest-supported position.
Trains the lats and biceps together for arm-and-back content efficiency.

name: Man Maker
summary: A dumbbell complex that chains a push-up, two renegade rows, a squat clean and an overhead press into one rep.
instructions: Set two dumbbells on the floor about shoulder-width apart and take a high plank with one hand on each handle.
Lower your chest toward the dumbbells and press back up, keeping your hips level and your feet wide enough to stay stable.
Row the right dumbbell to your ribs without letting the hips rotate, lower it under control, then repeat on the left.
Step or jump both feet up outside your hands so you finish in a deep squat with the dumbbells still on the floor.
Stand and clean both dumbbells to your shoulders, then press them overhead until your elbows lock out.
Lower the dumbbells to your shoulders and back to the floor, then return to the plank to start the next repetition.
mistakes: Letting the hips rotate during the row, which turns the plank into a twist and pulls load off the working side.
Setting the feet too narrow in the plank, which makes the base unstable and forces you to cut the row short.
Flaring the ribs and arching the spine on the press, which shifts load off the shoulders and onto the lower back.
Chaining the four parts together before each one is clean, which is the fastest way to lose form once fatigue arrives.
benefits: Covers push, pull, squat and press patterns inside a single repetition, so a short set does a lot of work.
Drives heart rate high with nothing but a pair of dumbbells, which suits circuits with limited floor space.
Exposes trunk stability under fatigue, because the rows require anti-rotation control mid-set.

name: MB Throw
summary: An overhead medicine-ball throw from a staggered stance, whipping the ball forward into a wall or a partner.
instructions: Stand in a staggered stance facing a wall or partner, holding a medicine ball in both hands.
Brace the trunk and keep the eyes on the target.
Swing the ball overhead and bend the elbows so it sits behind the head.
Shift weight onto the back leg as you load the throw.
Step forward and throw the ball by extending the hips, knees, and arms together.
Catch the rebound or reset, then repeat without collapsing the ribs.
mistakes: Throwing a ball that is too heavy to move fast, which turns the throw into a slow press.
Arching the lower back as the ball goes behind the head.
Leaving the legs quiet so the arms do all of the work.
Standing so far from the wall that the rebound cannot be caught.
benefits: Trains upper-body rate of force with a throw instead of a grind.
The staggered stance links a step to the overhead release.
A wall rebound lets you repeat throws without a partner.

name: Meadows Row
summary: A unilateral landmine row taken from a staggered stance side-on to the bar, pulling one side of the back.
instructions: Wedge one end of a barbell into a landmine or a corner and load the other end.
Stand beside the loaded end so your body is side-on to the bar.
Stagger your stance with the leg nearest the bar set behind you.
Hinge forward and grip the bar end overhand with your shoulder above it.
Row the bar back toward your hip, letting the elbow flare and pass your torso.
Lower to a full stretch, finish the set, then switch sides.
mistakes: Squaring up to the bar, which turns the sweeping arc into an ordinary bent over row.
Twisting the torso to lift the weight, which trades back work for spinal rotation.
Standing too upright, so the range shortens and the lats barely stretch.
Losing the thick sleeve to grip fatigue, which ends the set before the back is worked.
benefits: Trains one side of the back at a time so asymmetry shows up.
The long rowing arc keeps the lats loaded through a full stretch.
The staggered stance adds an anti-rotation demand on the trunk.

name: Mountain Climber
summary: A high-tempo plank-position knee drive that trains the core and spikes the heart rate — the universal HIIT finisher.
instructions: Set up in a high-plank position with your hands directly under your shoulders and arms locked out.
Brace your core hard and squeeze your glutes to keep your hips level with your shoulders.
Drive your right knee toward your chest, keeping the foot off the floor at the front of the motion.
Snap the right leg back as you drive the left knee forward in a smooth, alternating rhythm.
Keep the hips low and the shoulders stacked over the wrists the entire set.
Continue for 20 to 40 seconds at a controlled pace, prioritizing form over raw speed.
mistakes: Letting the hips bounce up and down, which removes the core demand and breaks the plank shape.
Sagging the lower back as the legs drive, which strains the spine instead of loading the core.
Putting the hands too far in front of the shoulders, which collapses the plank and stresses the wrists.
Going too fast and losing range of motion, with knees barely moving instead of driving toward the chest.
benefits: Trains the core under load while spiking the heart rate at the same time.
Builds full-body conditioning with zero equipment or space requirements.
Reinforces a strong plank shape under fatigue and movement.

name: Muscle-up
summary: A bar skill that links a high pull-up to a straight-bar dip, taking the body from a hang to locked-out support.
instructions: Hang from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip slightly wider than the shoulders.
Set an active hang with the legs together and the trunk braced.
Pull the bar toward the lower chest or stomach, keeping both sides even.
As the chest clears the bar, lean the shoulders forward and turn the wrists over together.
Press to straight-arm support with the torso stacked over the bar.
Lower under control through the dip and the hang, then reset.
mistakes: Pulling straight into the bar instead of creating a path around it.
Treating the lift as three frozen steps instead of one continuous path.
Starting with a normal pull-up grip that blocks the wrist turnover.
Attempting it before strict pull-ups and dips are strong enough to finish.
benefits: Links a high pull and a dip into one upper-body skill.
Builds grip, trunk stiffness, and coordination under a hang.
Is the competition skill many calisthenics and CrossFit programs need.

name: Narrow Pulldown
summary: A close-grip lat pulldown that bias-loads the lower lats and biceps — the narrow-grip take on the classic vertical pull.
instructions: Attach a close-grip V-handle to the cable and sit on the machine with your thighs locked under the pad.
Grip the handle with palms facing each other and let your arms extend fully overhead.
Lean your torso back about 10 to 15 degrees and pull your shoulder blades down to set the lats.
Pull the handle down to your upper chest by driving the elbows down close to the sides of your body.
Pause briefly at the bottom with the handle at your collarbones, squeezing the lower lats hard.
Let the handle travel slowly back overhead over 2 to 3 seconds until your arms are fully extended.
mistakes: Pulling with the biceps and forearms instead of leading with the elbows and back.
Leaning too far back so the lift turns into a row instead of a vertical pull.
Cutting the top range short and never letting the arms fully extend overhead.
Letting the stack snap up at the top, removing the slow return portion of each rep.
benefits: Bias-loads the lower lats with a narrow, biceps-friendly grip.
Trains the vertical pull through a longer range than the wide-grip version.
Adds variation to pulldown programming for balanced lat development.

name: Neck Curl
summary: Supine neck curl that trains the front of the neck by lifting the head against gravity through a short range.
instructions: Lie face up on a bench with your head just past the edge.
Rest your arms across your chest and keep your shoulders flat on the bench.
Let your head lower until you feel a light stretch at the front of the neck.
Tuck your chin slightly toward your chest and hold that position.
Curl your head up toward your chest without lifting your shoulders.
Pause at the top, then lower slowly through the full range and repeat.
mistakes: Jutting the chin forward instead of tucking it, which loads the upper neck joints.
Lifting the shoulders and trunk, which turns the movement into a partial crunch.
Adding load before the bodyweight range is smooth, which shifts work onto the superficial flexors.
Bobbing the head quickly, which produces range without controlled muscle work.
benefits: Trains neck flexion directly, which almost no other lift loads.
Builds head and neck control that matters in contact and combat sports.
Bodyweight loading and a short range make it easy to start and to progress slowly.

name: Neck Extension
summary: A prone neck extension done off the end of a bench, lifting the head against gravity to load the neck extensors.
instructions: Lie face down on a flat bench with your hips centered and your chest past the front edge.
Place your hands flat on the bench under your shoulders to support your upper body.
Let your head and neck hang past the edge with your face toward the floor.
Lift your head back until your neck lines up with your upper back.
Hold the top for a beat with your jaw and shoulders relaxed.
Lower your head slowly to the start and repeat for the prescribed reps.
mistakes: Throwing the head back into full hyperextension, which jams the neck joints instead of loading the extensors.
Adding load before the neck can hold a clean range, which turns the set into a jerky swing.
Shrugging the shoulders to help, which hides how much work the neck is actually doing.
Letting the chest lift off the bench, so the movement becomes a back extension instead of a neck extension.
benefits: Loads the neck extensors directly, a group most training plans never address.
Needs only a bench, so it fits home, gym and clinic settings alike.
The short bodyweight range makes the effort easy to scale by tempo and reps.

name: Neutral-Grip Dumbbell Bench Press
summary: Flat dumbbell press with the palms facing each other, keeping the elbows tucked and the wrists neutral.
instructions: Sit on the end of a flat bench holding a dumbbell in each hand with palms facing inward.
Rest the dumbbells on your thighs, then lie back and bring them to chest level.
Set your shoulder blades back into the bench and plant both feet on the floor.
Press the dumbbells up until your arms are nearly straight, keeping palms facing each other.
Lower them under control until the handles reach chest level, keeping your elbows close to your sides.
Repeat for the prescribed reps, then bring your knees up to help you sit back up safely.
mistakes: Letting the elbows drift wide loses the neutral-grip advantage and returns stress to the front of the shoulder.
Clashing the dumbbells together at the top unloads the chest and risks losing control of one hand.
Locking the elbows hard at the top drops tension off the pectorals between reps.
Dropping the dumbbells to the floor from the finished position strains the shoulders on the way out of the set.
benefits: Neutral wrist and elbow position is usually easier to tolerate than a pronated grip for sore shoulders.
Tucked elbow path recruits the triceps more than a standard dumbbell press.
Each arm works independently, which exposes and evens out side-to-side differences.

name: Neutral-Grip Lat Pulldown
summary: A cable pulldown pulled on a V-bar with palms facing each other, keeping the shoulders and wrists neutral.
instructions: Clip a V-bar or parallel handle onto the high pulley of a pulldown station.
Sit down and lock your thighs under the pad.
Take the handle with palms facing each other and straighten your arms.
Pull your shoulder blades down and keep your chest tall.
Draw the handle to your upper chest with your elbows tracking close to your ribs.
Return slowly until your arms are fully extended and repeat.
mistakes: Rocking the torso back and forth, which turns the pulldown into a partial row.
Shrugging at the start, so the upper traps absorb the load before the lats.
Curling the handle down with the arms, which makes the biceps the limiting factor.
Cutting the top of the range short, which removes the loaded lat stretch.
benefits: Neutral forearms keep the shoulder out of full internal rotation.
Comfortable grip for lifters with wrist or elbow sensitivity.
Delivers lat activation comparable to pronated pulldown grips.

name: Neutral-Grip Pull-Up
summary: A bodyweight pull-up performed on parallel handles with palms facing each other, easier on the shoulders.
instructions: Hook a V-bar or parallel handles over a pull-up bar.
Grip the handles so your palms face each other and hang with straight arms.
Brace your core and squeeze your glutes to stop your legs swinging.
Pull your shoulder blades down and back to begin the movement.
Drive your elbows toward your ribs until your chest reaches the handles.
Lower under control to a near-straight hang and repeat.
mistakes: Kipping or swinging the legs, which reduces the load the back actually handles.
Pulling only with the arms, so the biceps fail before the lats are trained.
Stopping partway up, which limits the contraction at the top of the range.
Dropping into a hard dead hang each rep, which stresses the elbows and shoulders.
benefits: Neutral shoulder position reduces impingement risk versus a wide pronated grip.
Strong biceps and brachialis contribution makes the pull feel achievable.
Needs only a bar and a handle, so it fits minimal-equipment programs.

name: Nordic Hamstring Curl
summary: A kneeling bodyweight curl where the hamstrings resist the whole body lowering toward the floor under eccentric control.
instructions: Kneel on a pad with your knees bent and the tops of your feet flat on the floor.
Anchor your ankles under a loaded barbell, a fixed pad, or a partner's hands.
Stand tall through the hips so knees, hips and shoulders form one line.
Reach your arms forward and lower your torso slowly, keeping the hips extended.
Catch yourself on your hands once you can no longer control the descent.
Push back just enough to let the hamstrings pull you upright, then repeat.
mistakes: Breaking at the hips so the movement becomes a bow, which unloads the hamstrings.
Dropping fast once it gets hard, which removes the eccentric stimulus the exercise exists for.
Pushing hard off the floor every rep, so the arms do the work the hamstrings should.
Starting at full range with no assistance, which usually ends in a cramp or a strain.
benefits: Loads the hamstrings eccentrically at the long lengths where strains occur.
Needs only an ankle anchor, so it travels to any field, gym or garage.
Progresses by range and tempo rather than by adding external load.

name: One Arm Dumbbell Bench Press
summary: A supine one-dumbbell press from a flat bench, lowering beside the chest and locking out over the shoulder.
instructions: Sit at the end of a flat bench with one dumbbell on the thigh, then lie back and press it to lockout.
Plant both feet and keep the back, shoulders, and hips on the bench.
Hold the free hand near the hip or on the bench; it does not hold a weight.
Lower the dumbbell beside the chest until the elbow is about ninety degrees, forearm vertical.
Press it straight up over the working shoulder until the elbow is long.
Finish the set, then switch arms and match the same range.
mistakes: Letting the torso roll toward the working arm as the bell comes down.
Flaring the elbow into a wide arc instead of a narrow up-and-down press.
Bouncing the dumbbell off the chest at the bottom.
Starting on the stronger side and leaving the weaker side undertrained.
benefits: Trains each side on its own so a weaker press cannot hide.
Forces the trunk to resist rotation under a single load.
Uses one dumbbell and a flat bench, so it fits small-gym templates.

name: One Leg Barbell Squat
summary: A rear-foot-elevated split squat with a barbell on the back, descending on the front leg until the thigh is near parallel.
instructions: Set a low box behind you and unrack a barbell onto the upper back.
Place the rear foot on the box and plant the front foot far enough forward to squat without the knee collapsing.
Brace the trunk and keep the front heel down.
Lower by bending the front knee until the thigh is near parallel, rear knee traveling toward the floor.
Drive through the front foot to stand without locking the knee hard at the top.
Finish the set, then switch legs and match the same depth.
mistakes: Setting the rear foot too high, which dumps the low back into extension.
Letting the front knee cave inward on the way down.
Leaning the torso far forward so the lift becomes a hinge.
Starting heavy before a bodyweight or dumbbell version is stable.
benefits: Loads one leg at a time so a weaker squat cannot hide.
The elevated rear foot lets you squat deep on the front leg without a hanging pistol.
A barbell on the back scales the lift past what most people can goblet.

name: One-Arm Incline Lateral Raise
summary: A side-lying one-arm raise on an incline bench, lifting a dumbbell from the hip toward shoulder height.
instructions: Set an incline bench and lie on your side along the pad with the working arm hanging free.
Hold one dumbbell in the lower hand with a neutral grip and a slight bend in the elbow.
Brace the free hand on the top of the bench and keep the torso quiet on the pad.
Raise the dumbbell out to the side until the arm is about parallel to the floor.
Pause without shrugging the working shoulder toward the ear.
Lower under control to the hang and repeat, then switch sides.
mistakes: Raising the bell past shoulder height, which hands the work to the traps.
Rolling the torso off the pad to heave the weight up.
Straightening the elbow so the joint takes the load.
Using a standing hip swing that the bench was meant to remove.
benefits: The incline pad blocks torso swing so the side deltoid has to lift the load.
One arm at a time makes left-to-right gaps obvious.
A light dumbbell and a short range make it a clean isolation clip.

name: One-Arm Kettlebell Military Press To Side
summary: A standing one-arm kettlebell press from the rack to an overhead lockout just beside the head.
instructions: Stand tall with the feet about hip-width apart and one kettlebell in the front rack.
Rest the bell on the forearm, wrist stacked, free arm hanging at the side.
Brace the trunk and keep the ribs stacked over the pelvis.
Press the kettlebell up and slightly out so it clears the head and locks out overhead.
Pause with the biceps near the ear and the shoulder packed, not shrugged.
Lower to the rack under control, finish the set, then switch sides.
mistakes: Leaning hard away from the bell to finish the press.
Letting the wrist fold back under the handle.
Jutting the head forward as the bell goes up.
Pressing the bell far out in front instead of stacking it over the shoulder.
benefits: Trains each shoulder on its own so a weaker press cannot hide.
The hanging bell challenges wrist and shoulder stability more than a dumbbell.
Standing setup needs only one kettlebell and floor space.

name: Open Book Rotation
summary: A side-lying thoracic rotation that opens the top arm across the body while the stacked knees stay down.
instructions: Lie on your side with hips and knees bent and a folded towel under your head.
Stack both arms in front of the chest at about shoulder height.
Keep the knees glued together so the pelvis stays on its side.
Sweep the top arm in a wide arc across the chest and open toward the floor behind you.
Let the head and eyes follow the moving hand as the chest turns up.
Return the top hand to the bottom hand and repeat, then switch sides.
mistakes: Letting the top knee lift, which rotates the hips instead of the mid-back.
Pushing only the hand behind you while the chest stays closed.
Forcing the top shoulder to the floor through a painful range.
Leaving the head facing forward instead of turning with the arm.
benefits: Trains thoracic rotation while the stacked knees keep the lumbar spine quiet.
Needs no kit beyond a towel, so it fits warm-ups anywhere.
Pairs well with overhead and rotational lifting as a daily reset.

name: Open Book Rotations
summary: A mat-based side-lying open book, rotating the top arm and head while stacked knees stay on the floor.
instructions: Lie on your side on a mat with hips and knees bent and two folded towels under your head.
Reach both arms forward at chest height with the palms together.
Pin the stacked knees to the mat so the pelvis cannot roll.
Sweep the top arm in a wide arc toward the opposite side as the chest opens.
Rotate the head with the moving hand so the gaze follows the arc.
Return the top hand to the bottom hand and repeat, then switch sides.
mistakes: Letting the top knee lift off the mat and rotating from the hips.
Freezing the head while the arm travels, so the chest never opens.
Bending the top elbow instead of sweeping a long arm.
Forcing the top shoulder to the floor through a painful range.
benefits: The mat and head towels make the drill easy to repeat in a studio setup.
Stacked knees keep lumbar rotation out of a thoracic mobility clip.
Head-follows-hand cuing is visible for coaching in an app loop.

name: Pallof Press
summary: A standing anti-rotation drill: hold a cable or band at chest height side-on and press it out without letting the torso turn.
instructions: Set a cable pulley or anchor a band at chest height.
Stand side-on to the anchor and take the handle in both hands with your fingers laced.
Step away until the cable is under tension and set your feet slightly wider than shoulder width.
Pull the handle in to the center of your chest and brace your abs hard.
Press the handle straight out and hold for two to three seconds without letting your torso turn.
Return the handle to your chest under control, finish the set, then turn around and face the other way.
mistakes: Letting the hips and shoulders rotate toward the anchor, which removes the anti-rotation demand entirely.
Standing too close to the stack, so there is no tension left to resist at full extension.
Holding your breath through the press, which usually means the load is beyond what your bracing can hold.
Pressing off-center or across the body, which turns the drill into an unsteady one-arm chest press.
benefits: Trains the trunk to resist rotation rather than produce it.
Isometric bracing loads the obliques and deep abdominals without spinal flexion.
Scales cleanly by stepping closer to or further from the anchor.

name: Parallel Bar Dips
summary: A bodyweight dip on parallel bars that builds the chest and triceps — one of the most demanding pure-bodyweight upper-body lifts.
instructions: Grip the parallel bars with palms facing each other and press up to a strong, locked-out start position.
Brace your core, squeeze the glutes, and cross the ankles to keep the body in a tight line.
Lean your torso slightly forward to bias the chest, or stay upright to bias the triceps.
Lower yourself slowly over 2 to 3 seconds until your shoulders drop just below your elbows.
Pause briefly at the bottom with the chest open and the body still controlled.
Press back up to full lockout by driving through the chest and triceps in one smooth motion.
mistakes: Letting the shoulders shrug up to the ears at the bottom, which strains the front shoulders.
Cutting the depth short and only doing the easy top half of the rep.
Swinging the legs to use momentum, which removes the controlled loading the dip is meant to deliver.
Flaring the elbows wide on the press, which puts unnecessary strain on the joint.
benefits: Builds serious chest, triceps, and front-shoulder strength with bodyweight only.
Trains a vertical press pattern that complements overhead and bench work.
Develops the body-control needed for advanced calisthenics.

name: Pause Squat
summary: A bodyweight squat held still at the bottom, removing the bounce so the legs restart from a dead stop.
instructions: Stand with your feet slightly wider than hip width and toes turned out a little.
Pull your shoulders down and back and brace your trunk.
Push the hips back and bend the knees together to descend.
Lower until your thighs are at least parallel, keeping the heels down.
Hold the bottom position for about a second without relaxing.
Press through the whole foot to stand and reset before the next rep.
mistakes: Relaxing in the bottom position, which lets the chest fold forward on the way up.
Bouncing out of the pause, which is the exact reflex the hold is meant to remove.
Letting the heels lift, which shifts load onto the front of the knees.
Holding far longer than a second, which fatigues the position instead of training it.
benefits: Removes the stretch reflex, so the legs produce every bit of the force.
Builds control and bracing at depth before external load is added.
Needs no equipment, so it scales any bodyweight lower body plan.

name: Pendlay Row
summary: A barbell row reset on the floor each rep, pulled explosively from a dead stop to the abdomen.
instructions: Set a loaded barbell on the floor directly in front of your shins.
Bend forward at the hips until your back is almost level above the bar.
Take a double overhand grip just outside your knees.
Brace your abdominals and set your shoulder blades before pulling.
Pull the bar explosively to your belly button, driving your elbows back.
Return the bar to the floor, let it settle, then start the next rep.
mistakes: Bouncing the bar off the floor, which removes the dead stop the exercise is built around.
Raising the torso as the bar comes up, so the hips finish the lift instead of the back.
Rounding the lower back on the reset, which loads the lumbar spine at the worst moment.
Pulling slowly, which turns a power exercise into an ordinary heavy row.
benefits: Every rep starts from a dead stop, so no momentum carries over.
Trains explosive pulling strength for the lats and mid back.
Reinforces the hinge position under repeated heavy loading.

name: Pendulum Squat / V-Squat
summary: A machine squat on a counterbalanced arc, keeping the torso supported while the quads work through deep range.
instructions: Load the machine and set the foot plate to suit your height and ankle range.
Position your back and shoulders against the pads with your hips settled.
Place your feet hip to shoulder width on the plate, toes turned out slightly.
Release the safeties and brace your trunk.
Descend along the arc until your thighs pass parallel.
Drive through the feet to return, stopping just short of knee lockout.
mistakes: Letting the head and hips fall out of line, which twists the load off the arc.
Riding the machine down quickly, which wastes the loaded stretch at the bottom.
Letting the heels lift off the plate, which shifts the load onto the knees.
Skipping the warm-up before loading a deep, stretched squat position.
benefits: The arc keeps tension high in the stretched position where quad growth is driven.
Back support removes spinal loading from a deep squat pattern.
The guided path lets you train close to failure without a spotter.

name: Pike Push-Up/Handstand Push-Up
summary: A floor pike press from an inverted V, lowering the head toward the hands to load the shoulders like an overhead press.
instructions: Set both hands on the floor about shoulder width and lift the hips into an inverted V.
Keep the legs long, heels reaching down, and the head hanging between the arms.
Brace the trunk so the pike does not sag.
Bend the elbows about 45 degrees from the body and lower the head toward the floor.
Stop when the head is close to the hands without collapsing the shoulders.
Press through the palms to straight arms and return to the pike.
mistakes: Letting the hips sag, which turns the pike into a regular push-up.
Flaring the elbows wide and stressing the shoulder joint.
Rushing the lowering phase instead of controlling both halves of the press.
Lifting the head and cranking the neck to look forward.
benefits: Shifts a push-up into a vertical press so the deltoids take the load.
Needs no equipment, which makes it a home overhead-press stand-in.
Builds the pressing strength that later progressions take to a wall handstand.

name: Pistol Squat
summary: A full-depth squat on one leg with the free leg held straight out in front as a counterbalance.
instructions: Stand on one leg with the other leg straight out in front and the supporting knee slightly bent.
Reach both arms forward and keep your weight over the middle of the supporting foot.
Sit the hips down and back as the supporting knee flexes, chest staying tall.
Descend until the working hamstring meets the calf, or stop if the lower back rounds.
Pause with the free leg still off the floor.
Drive the heel down to stand, then switch legs.
mistakes: Letting the supporting knee collapse inward at the bottom.
Rounding the lower back to force depth the hips do not have.
Dropping into the hole on momentum instead of controlling the descent.
Letting the free leg sag toward the floor and turning the lift into a partial squat.
benefits: Builds equal single-leg strength because each side has to finish the same depth.
Trains balance, ankle dorsiflexion, and trunk stiffness with no extra load.
Is a clear advanced benchmark for bodyweight lower-body programs.

name: Pistol Squat (Assisted)
summary: A single-leg squat to depth with the free leg held forward, using a vertical pole only as light balance.
instructions: Stand tall on one leg facing a sturdy vertical pole, with the free leg extended forward and the toes pulled up.
Grip the pole at about chest height with both hands, using it only as light balance.
Keep the standing heel down and the chest tall as you sit the hips back and bend the standing knee.
Lower until the standing hamstring is close to the calf, or as deep as a neutral spine allows.
Drive through the standing foot to stand back up without yanking on the pole.
Finish tall on the same leg, then switch sides after the set.
mistakes: Pulling the body up with the arms instead of using the pole only for balance.
Letting the standing heel rise, which dumps the knee forward and cuts depth.
Dropping the free foot to the floor or bending that knee to cheat the balance.
Collapsing the standing knee inward instead of tracking it over the toes.
benefits: Builds single-leg squat strength with a light balance aid so the full pistol shape is trainable.
Keeps the heel down more easily than an unassisted pistol while ankle mobility is still limited.
Lets coaches progress from a full-hand grip to two fingers to a free-standing pistol.

name: Plate Forward Lunge
summary: A forward lunge holding a weight plate at the chest that loads the quads and glutes through a single-leg step — the gym-floor classic.
instructions: Stand tall holding a weight plate horizontally against your upper chest with both hands.
Brace your core, pull your shoulders back, and set your feet hip-width apart.
Step one foot forward into a long stride, lowering your back knee toward the floor.
Stop when your front thigh is roughly parallel to the floor and your back knee hovers above it.
Drive through the heel of your front foot to push back to the standing start position.
Repeat on the opposite leg, alternating sides for the full set with the plate locked at the chest.
mistakes: Letting the front knee cave inward on the step, which strains the joint and reduces force production.
Taking a stride that's too short, which puts the front knee far past the toes and overloads it.
Leaning the torso forward over the plate instead of staying upright through the descent.
Pushing off the back foot to stand up, which steals work from the front leg the lunge is meant to load.
benefits: Builds quad and glute strength with a single-leg pattern that fixes side imbalances.
Trains the core to brace under a front-loaded position.
Easy to scale up by simply choosing a heavier plate.

name: Plate Front Raise
summary: A front raise holding one weight plate at the three and nine o'clock positions and lifting it to shoulder height.
instructions: Pick up a weight plate and hold it at the three and nine o'clock positions with your palms facing each other.
Stand tall with your feet hip-width apart and your shoulders pulled back.
Let the plate hang a few inches in front of your thighs without touching them.
Brace your abs and keep a slight bend in your elbows.
Raise the plate in front of you until it is just above parallel with the floor, then pause.
Lower it slowly back to the start without letting it rest against your body.
mistakes: Swinging the plate up with a hip drive, which removes the front of the deltoid from the lift.
Letting the plate touch the thighs between reps, which unloads the shoulder at the bottom.
Gripping too low on the plate, so it tips away from the wrists and the set ends on grip.
Programming it only alongside heavy pressing, which piles more volume on an already busy anterior deltoid.
benefits: One plate is all the equipment needed, which suits crowded or minimally kitted gyms.
The neutral two-handed grip keeps the wrists in a comfortable position.
Strict single-joint work makes front deltoid volume easy to count in a program.

name: Plate Pinch
summary: Static grip hold in which you pinch a pair of weight plates between the thumb and flat fingers for time.
instructions: Stand one or two plates on end with the smooth sides facing out.
Set your thumb on one face and your flat fingers on the other, avoiding any hook around the rim.
Squeeze the plates together and stand up tall with the arm hanging at your side.
Keep your shoulder packed and your wrist neutral, with no swinging.
Hold until the grip is about to fail, aiming for twenty to thirty seconds.
Set the plates down under control and repeat with the other hand.
mistakes: Hooking the fingers around the plate rim, which turns a pinch into a hold and removes the thumb demand.
Letting the wrist bend under load, which cuts pinch force before the fingers actually fatigue.
Swinging the arm to reduce the felt load, which shortens the useful time under tension.
Programming it before heavy pulling work, which leaves grip fatigued for the main lifts.
benefits: Trains thumb-to-finger pinch strength that crushing-grip work does not reach.
Simple to load and progress by adding plates or thinner plate stacks.
Requires almost no space or setup, so it fits at the end of any session.

name: Plyo Kettlebell Pushups
summary: An explosive push-up that alternates sides of one fixed kettlebell, switching the hand on the handle.
instructions: Place one stable kettlebell on a level surface with room on either side.
Take a plank position with one hand gripping the handle and the other palm on the floor.
Brace the trunk and bend the elbows to lower the chest.
Press explosively to move the upper body laterally across the fixed bell.
Switch hands so the opposite hand grips the handle and the free palm lands on the floor.
Settle into the new support position and perform the next push-up before switching again.
mistakes: Letting the lower back sag during the press.
Flaring the upper arms straight out to the sides.
Losing a secure hand contact when landing.
Allowing the kettlebell to tip or travel during the switch.
benefits: Trains explosive upper-body pressing.
Challenges trunk control during a moving plank.
Adds an alternating hand-support pattern to push-up practice.

name: Pogo Hops
summary: Low, quick in-place hops on stiff ankles, using the calves and Achilles as a spring with almost no knee bend.
instructions: Stand tall with the feet hip-width and the arms relaxed at your sides.
Rise onto the balls of the feet with the knees almost straight.
Hop in place by pushing through the ankles, not by sitting into a squat.
Pull the toes toward the shins in the air so the next contact is springy.
Land quietly under the hips and rebound right away.
Keep the torso tall and repeat for short, fast contacts.
mistakes: Bending the knees into a mini squat so the hop is no longer ankle-dominant.
Chasing height instead of a low, quick pop off the floor.
Letting the heels slam and dump the spring out of the Achilles.
Reaching the feet out in front of the hips on landing.
benefits: Trains ankle stiffness and short ground contacts without a high jump.
Lets coaches keep plyometric work in a heavy week at a low amplitude.
Is an entry drill before higher-impact hops and bounds.

name: Power Clean - no overhead press
summary: An explosive barbell pull from the floor to a front rack catch on the shoulders, finishing without any overhead press.
instructions: Set a loaded barbell on the floor about an inch in front of your shins with your feet hip-width apart.
Squat down and grip the bar just outside your knees with your hips below your shoulders and your chest up.
Extend your hips and knees to lift the bar while keeping your torso angle and the bar close to your legs.
As the bar passes your knees, drive your hips forward and explosively extend hips, knees and ankles.
Shrug and pull your elbows high, then whip them under the bar to catch it on your front deltoids in a quarter squat.
Stand tall to finish the rep, then lower the bar back to the floor under control.
mistakes: Pulling with the arms early, which spends the leg drive that should be moving the bar.
Letting the bar drift away from the body, which throws the catch forward and out of position.
Catching with the elbows low, so the bar rolls onto the wrists instead of resting on the shoulders.
Loading it before the sequence is grooved, which turns an explosive lift into a slow bent-over row.
benefits: Trains triple extension of the hips, knees and ankles against a heavy external load.
The whole-body timing demand makes it a coordination lift as much as a strength lift.
It ends at the shoulders rather than overhead, so the shoulder demand stays low.

name: Press Sit-Up
summary: A floor sit-up holding a barbell at the chest, then pressing it overhead as the torso comes upright.
instructions: Lie on your back with knees bent and both feet anchored under a plate or similar stop.
Hold a light barbell at the chest with an overhand grip.
Brace the trunk and keep the bar stacked over the chest.
Sit up by curling the ribs toward the thighs.
As you reach the top, press the bar overhead to locked elbows.
Lower the bar to the chest, then roll the torso back to the floor.
mistakes: Yanking with the neck instead of curling the trunk.
Using a heavy bar that turns the sit-up into a hip-flexor heave.
Letting the feet fly so the hips slide and the press drifts.
Arching the lower back to finish the press instead of sitting tall.
benefits: Loads a sit-up so the abs can progress past bodyweight.
Adds an overhead press at the top without a second exercise.
The floor setup needs only a bar and a foot anchor.

name: Prone Lateral Raises
summary: A chest-supported reverse fly on an incline bench, raising two dumbbells out to the sides to load the rear delts.
instructions: Set an incline bench and lie chest-down with a dumbbell in each hand.
Let both arms hang toward the floor with a slight bend in the elbows.
Use a pronated grip so the palms face behind you at the start.
Raise both dumbbells out to the sides until the arms are about parallel to the floor.
Squeeze the rear delts at the top without shrugging the traps to the ears.
Lower under control and repeat without swinging the torso.
mistakes: Heaving the torso off the pad to swing the dumbbells up.
Bending the elbows into a row so the lats take the lift.
Using a load so heavy the arms cannot reach a long arc.
Shrugging the shoulders toward the ears and handing the work to the upper traps.
benefits: Chest support blocks body english so the rear delts have to lift.
Balances pressing-heavy shoulder work with a reverse fly.
Light dumbbells and a long lever make a small muscle easy to feel.

name: Prone Y-T Raises
summary: A floor scapular series that lifts both arms into a Y, then a T, to train the lower traps and rear delts.
instructions: Lie face down with the legs long and the forehead toward the floor.
Brace the trunk so the lower back stays quiet.
Reach both arms overhead at about 45 degrees to form a Y, thumbs up.
Lift the arms a few inches by drawing the shoulder blades down and back, then lower.
Move the arms out to the sides to form a T, thumbs still up, and lift again.
Lower with control and keep cycling Y and T without shrugging the ears.
mistakes: Arching the lower back to get the arms higher.
Shrugging the shoulders toward the ears instead of setting the blades down.
Rushing the lifts so the arms swing instead of hovering.
Turning the head to the side instead of keeping the face down.
benefits: Targets the lower traps and rear delts without a load.
The floor takes cheating out of scapular work.
Fits warm-ups before pressing or overhead skill work.

name: Prying Goblet Squat
summary: A kettlebell goblet squat that pauses in the hole so the elbows can pry the knees out and open the hips.
instructions: Stand with the feet about shoulder width and the toes turned out slightly.
Hold a kettlebell by the horns at the chest with the elbows pointing down.
Brace the trunk and pull yourself down between the knees.
At the bottom, slide the elbows inside the knees and pry the knees out.
Keep the chest tall and the heels down while you breathe in the hole.
Stand by driving the floor away, then reset the goblet before the next descent.
mistakes: Folding the lower back in the hole instead of keeping a long spine.
Resting on the joints with a soft trunk instead of prying against tension.
Prying on every heavy set after the hips are already open.
Letting the kettlebell drift away from the chest and losing the counterweight.
benefits: The front load lets most people sit deeper with a taller chest.
Elbows-in-knees prying opens the hips without a separate stretch.
It is the teaching squat used before heavier front squats.

name: Pull Ups
summary: The classic bodyweight vertical pull that builds the lats, biceps, and upper back — the benchmark for upper-body pulling strength.
instructions: Reach up and grip a fixed pull-up bar with palms facing forward, hands slightly wider than shoulders.
Hang from the bar with arms fully extended, then engage the lats by pulling the shoulder blades down.
Brace your core, squeeze the glutes, and cross the ankles to keep the body in a tight line.
Pull yourself up by driving the elbows down toward the ribs until your chin clears the bar.
Pause briefly at the top with the chin over the bar, squeezing the lats and upper back.
Lower yourself slowly over 2 to 3 seconds back to a full dead hang before the next rep.
mistakes: Kipping the legs to swing up instead of pulling cleanly with the back and arms.
Cutting the bottom range short and never reaching a full dead hang, which trains a fraction of the lift.
Leading with the chin instead of the chest, which puts strain on the neck.
Dropping fast at the top and skipping the slow descent, where most pull-up strength is built.
benefits: Builds the lats, biceps, and upper back with one of the highest-yield bodyweight lifts.
Develops the relative strength needed for advanced calisthenics and athletic work.
Reinforces shoulder health by training the back muscles that stabilize the joint.

name: Push Jerk
summary: Barbell overhead lift driven by a short leg dip, received in a partial squat with the feet planted.
instructions: Take the bar in a front rack across the shoulders with the elbows down and in front of the bar.
Set your feet in your squat stance with your weight balanced over the whole foot.
Brace your trunk and dip by bending the knees only, keeping the torso vertical.
Reverse hard and drive the bar off the shoulders with the legs.
Punch the elbows into lockout overhead and receive the bar in a partial squat with the feet planted.
Stand up with the bar stable overhead, then lower it back to the rack position.
mistakes: Dipping too deep, which slows the reversal and turns the lift into a slow press.
Letting the torso pitch forward in the dip, which sends the bar out in front of the body.
Pressing with the arms before the legs finish, which loses the drive and stalls the bar at eye level.
Receiving with soft elbows, which puts the load on the shoulder joint instead of the skeleton.
benefits: Moves heavier overhead loads than a strict press by adding leg drive.
Trains the dip and drive timing that transfers to the split jerk.
Builds overhead lockout strength and stability under speed.

name: Push Up
summary: The most foundational bodyweight push lift — trains the chest, triceps, and front shoulders with a single, scalable pattern.
instructions: Set up in a high-plank position with your hands slightly wider than shoulder width and arms locked.
Brace your core, squeeze the glutes, and keep your body in a straight line from head to heels.
Lower your chest slowly toward the floor over 2 to 3 seconds, keeping the elbows at about 45 degrees.
Stop when your chest hovers just above the floor, holding the bottom briefly with full body tension.
Press back up by driving the floor away through the palms until the arms reach full extension.
Reset your breath and repeat for the full set, keeping the body line tight on every rep.
mistakes: Letting the hips sag toward the floor, which removes the core demand and strains the lower back.
Letting the elbows flare to 90 degrees, which strains the front shoulders and reduces chest engagement.
Cutting the depth short and only pressing the top half of the rep instead of touching the chest down.
Letting the head poke forward instead of keeping the neck in line with the spine.
benefits: Builds the chest, triceps, and front shoulders without any equipment.
Reinforces a strong full-body plank shape under pressing load.
Scales infinitely from incline beginner versions to advanced weighted variations.

name: Push-Up Wide
summary: A floor push-up with the hands set outside the shoulders, biasing the press toward the chest through a deeper stretch at the bottom.
instructions: Get on all fours with the hands set wider than the shoulders and the toes tucked.
Straighten both legs into a high plank so the body makes one line from head to heels.
Look at the floor, lock the elbows, and brace the trunk before you lower.
Bend the elbows and let the chest drop while the shoulder blades slide on the ribcage.
Stop when the upper arms sit about even with the floor or the chest is close to the ground.
Push the floor away until the elbows straighten and the chest returns to the start.
mistakes: Letting the arms form a T at the bottom instead of an arrow, which loads the shoulders.
Letting the hips sag because the trunk was never braced before the first repetition.
Setting the hands as wide as they will go, which cuts range and opens the shoulders further.
Stopping short at the top instead of pushing through and letting the shoulder blades move.
benefits: Biases a bodyweight press toward the chest and stretches the pecs at the bottom.
Needs no equipment, so it drops into chest, push, and full-body sessions anywhere.
Scales by tempo and foot elevation long before any external load is required.

name: Quadruped Thoracic Rotation
summary: A hands-and-knees mobility drill that rotates the mid-back while one hand stays planted and the other tracks the elbow.
instructions: Kneel on all fours with the knees under the hips and one hand planted under the same-side shoulder.
Place the free hand on the back of the head with that elbow tucked down toward the planted arm.
Brace the trunk so the hips stay level and stacked over the knees.
Rotate the ribcage and lift the moving elbow toward the ceiling, letting the head follow.
Pause when the chest opens without the hips rolling or the planted arm collapsing.
Reverse the same path until the elbow tucks again, then repeat before switching sides.
mistakes: Letting the hips twist with the ribcage, which turns a thoracic drill into a lumbar sway.
Pulling on the neck with the hand instead of using the hand as a light head rest.
Rushing the open position so the planted shoulder shrugs or the supporting elbow bends.
Starting with the elbow already pointed at the ceiling, which skips the closed-to-open range.
benefits: Trains thoracic rotation while the hips stay quiet on all fours.
Opens the chest and upper back after long periods of sitting.
Needs no equipment, so it fits warm-up blocks and home mobility pages.

name: Reverse Crunch
summary: A supine abdominal curl that rolls the hips off the floor and brings the bent knees up and over the chest.
instructions: Lie face up on a mat with your arms out to the sides, palms down, for balance.
Lift your feet and raise the knees until they sit directly over the hips, still bent about ninety degrees.
Brace the abdominals and press the lower back toward the mat before the first repetition.
Exhale and roll the hips toward the ribcage so the knees travel toward the head.
Pause at the top without changing the knee angle or swinging the legs.
Inhale and lower the hips back until the pelvis and spine rest on the mat, keeping the feet off the floor.
mistakes: Swinging the legs and riding momentum instead of curling the pelvis with the abdominals.
Changing the knee angle during the roll, which turns the drill into a hip-flexor kick.
Letting the feet drop to the floor between repetitions, which resets the tension every rep.
Dropping the hips back down rather than resisting the descent, which discards the eccentric.
benefits: Trains the abdominals from the pelvis upward, complementing the shoulder-led crunch.
Keeps the knees bent and the lever short, so the lower back stays supported.
Needs no equipment beyond floor space, so it fits home and travel programming.

name: Reverse Grip Barbell Curl
summary: A standing barbell curl taken with the palms facing down, shifting the work from the biceps onto the forearms.
instructions: Load a barbell and stand upright with your feet about hip-width apart.
Grip the bar palms down with your hands roughly shoulder-width apart.
Let the bar rest at your thighs with your elbows straight and pinned to your sides.
Curl the bar up by bending only at the elbows, keeping your wrists straight.
Stop when the bar reaches chest height and hold the top briefly.
Lower the bar under control to full extension and repeat.
mistakes: Loading it like a standard curl, which collapses the wrists long before the forearms are trained.
Letting the wrists bend back under the bar, which moves the strain to the wrist joint.
Swinging the elbows forward, which turns the lift into a front raise.
Rocking the torso to start each rep, so momentum replaces the elbow flexors.
benefits: Puts the forearm elbow flexors in their strongest pulling position.
Builds the grip and wrist strength that carries into rows and deadlifts.
Adds forearm thickness that palms-up curls alone tend to miss.

name: Reverse Hack Squat
summary: A hack squat performed facing the machine, shifting the squat pattern onto the glutes and hamstrings.
instructions: Load the machine and step onto the platform facing the pad.
Rest your chest on the pad with your shoulders under the shoulder pads.
Set your feet at shoulder width, slightly higher on the platform.
Extend the legs, release the safeties and take the load.
Push the hips back and lower until the knees reach about 90 degrees.
Drive through the heels to return without locking the knees.
mistakes: Keeping the torso vertical, which turns it back into a quad-dominant hack squat.
Letting the knees track well past the toes, which loads the joint and drops hip involvement.
Locking out at the top, which unloads the glutes and hamstrings between reps.
Dropping into the bottom, which loads the hamstrings faster than they can control.
benefits: Loads the glutes and hamstrings on a machine most gyms already own.
The chest pad supports the trunk, so the lower back is not the limiting factor.
Gives a second, posterior chain exercise from a single piece of equipment.

name: Reverse Hyperextension
summary: A prone hip extension off the end of a bench, lifting the legs behind the body to drive the glutes and hamstrings.
instructions: Lie face down on a flat bench with your hip crease at the front edge.
Let both legs hang toward the floor with your knees softly bent.
Reach under the bench and grip the frame so your torso cannot slide forward.
Squeeze your glutes and lift your legs behind you until your body is level.
Pause at the top without arching your lower back past flat.
Lower your legs slowly back to the hang and repeat for the prescribed reps.
mistakes: Swinging the legs so momentum carries them up, which unloads the glutes entirely.
Arching past level at the top, which shifts the load onto the lumbar spine.
Sliding forward so the hips are supported by the bench, which kills the range.
Leading with the lower back instead of the glutes, which is what makes it feel like a back exercise.
benefits: Trains hip extension with the torso supported, so the lower back is not the limiter.
Needs only a bench, so it works in home and minimal-equipment settings.
Builds the glute and hamstring strength that carries into hinges and squats.

name: Reverse Pec Deck
summary: Chest-supported machine fly performed in reverse, opening the arms backward to load the rear deltoids.
instructions: Set the seat height so the handles sit level with your shoulders and select a light load.
Sit facing the machine with your chest against the pad and your feet flat on the floor.
Take a handle in each hand with a pronated or neutral grip and hold a fixed bend in the elbows.
Sweep both arms out and back until they reach roughly shoulder height in line with your torso.
Hold the end position for a beat without shrugging or pushing your head forward.
Return the handles slowly to the start under control, then repeat.
mistakes: Driving the movement by squeezing the shoulder blades turns a rear-delt fly into a rowing pattern.
Letting the head jut forward as the arms open loads the neck and signals a load that is too heavy.
Bending and straightening the elbows through the rep converts the fly into a partial row.
Pulling the chest off the pad to gain range restores the trunk demand the machine was chosen to remove.
benefits: Isolates the rear deltoid, a group that most pressing-heavy programs leave underworked.
Chest support removes the trunk stability demand of bent-over reverse fly variations.
Fixed path makes light, high-repetition shoulder work easy to standardize across users.

name: Reverse-Grip Barbell Bench Press
summary: Flat barbell press taken with an underhand grip, which shifts pressing emphasis toward the upper chest.
instructions: Set the rack height on a flat bench and load the bar conservatively for your first sets.
Lie back with your feet planted and take the bar with an underhand grip a little wider than shoulder width.
Set your shoulder blades into the bench, then unrack the bar with a spotter's help.
Lower the bar slowly to your mid-chest, keeping your wrists stacked over your forearms.
Pause without letting the bar rest on your chest, then press it back up.
Stop short of locking the elbows and keep your glutes and shoulder blades on the bench throughout.
mistakes: Unracking a supinated bar without a spotter risks losing it backward before the first rep is under control.
Letting the wrists bend back under load puts the bar behind the forearm and strains the wrist joint.
Loading it like a standard bench press overwhelms an unfamiliar grip and forces the form to break down.
Lifting the feet or hips off the bench to grind a rep removes the stable base the press depends on.
benefits: Increases upper chest and biceps involvement compared with a pronated grip on the same flat bench.
Gives a fresh pressing stimulus for lifters with no access to an adjustable incline bench.
Alters the wrist and shoulder position, which some lifters find kinder on a sore shoulder.

name: Reverse-Grip Tricep Pushdown
summary: A cable pushdown taken with the palms up, keeping the elbows tucked so the triceps extend the arm through a long range.
instructions: Set a straight bar on the high pulley of a cable stack and select your weight.
Face the machine and grip the bar palms up with your hands shoulder-width apart.
Pull your elbows in against your ribs and hinge forward very slightly.
Press the bar down by straightening your elbows, keeping your upper arms still.
Stop just short of lockout and hold the bottom for a beat.
Let the bar rise under control until your elbows are fully bent, then repeat.
mistakes: Letting the elbows travel forward, which hands the work to the lats and shortens the triceps range.
Locking the elbows hard at the bottom, which drops tension and stresses the joint.
Leaning the whole torso into the bar, so bodyweight rather than the triceps moves the stack.
Gripping too wide, which twists the wrists uncomfortably under a palms-up hold.
benefits: The tucked elbow lets the arm extend further behind the body than a standard pushdown.
Emphasizes the long head of the triceps without needing an overhead position.
The underhand grip reduces forearm involvement and eases stress on the elbow.

name: RKC Plank
summary: A high-tension forearm plank that braces the whole body for a short hold instead of a long, relaxed one.
instructions: Set a forearm plank with the elbows under the chest and the body in one line from head to heels.
Clasp the hands together in front of the elbows, or keep the forearms parallel if that feels more stable.
Squeeze the legs together, lock the knees, and tuck the pelvis by squeezing the glutes.
Pull the elbows toward the toes and the toes toward the elbows without letting either end slide.
Breathe while holding that tension for a short effort, about ten to twenty seconds.
Release, reset the line, and repeat rather than hanging on in a sagging plank.
mistakes: Holding a relaxed plank for time instead of creating whole-body tension.
Letting the hips sag or pike, which dumps the load into the lower back.
Shrugging the shoulders toward the ears instead of packing them down.
Holding the breath, which makes the brace fail as soon as you need to inhale.
benefits: Raises abdominal and oblique demand well above a standard forearm plank.
Trains a posterior pelvic tilt and glute brace that carry into hinging lifts.
Needs no equipment and works in short, high-effort holds.

name: Romanian Deadlift from Deficit
summary: A Romanian deadlift performed standing on low plates so the bar can travel past the usual floor stop.
instructions: Stand with each foot on a low plate, feet about hip width, holding a barbell against the thighs.
Lock the hips and knees at the top, brace the trunk, and set the shoulder blades back.
Push the hips back and slide the bar down the front of the legs.
Keep only a slight knee bend and the bar in contact with the legs.
Stop where the hamstrings run out of stretch, then drive the hips forward to stand tall.
Finish stacked at the top without leaning back, and repeat.
mistakes: Rounding the lower back to chase extra depth the hamstrings cannot control.
Bending the knees into a squat, which unloads the hinge the deficit is there to lengthen.
Letting the bar drift off the legs, which lengthens the lever on the lumbar spine.
Using plates so high that the extra range cannot be owned with a neutral spine.
benefits: The small platform lengthens the eccentric so the hamstrings work through more stretch.
Teaches the same hip hinge as a standard RDL without pulling from the floor.
A lighter load still provides a hard posterior-chain stimulus because the range is longer.

name: Romanian Deadlift Hamstring Sweeps
summary: A standing bodyweight hinge with an arm sweep, taking the hamstrings through range as a dynamic warm-up.
instructions: Stand tall with your feet under your hips and your arms by your sides.
Step one foot forward and set the heel down with the toes lifted.
Keep both legs close to straight and brace your trunk lightly.
Hinge at the hips and sweep both arms down toward the front foot.
Sweep the arms back up as you drive the hips forward to stand.
Step through onto the other foot and repeat, alternating sides.
mistakes: Rounding the back to reach lower, which stretches the spine rather than the hamstrings.
Bending the front knee, which takes the hamstring out of the stretch entirely.
Bouncing at the bottom, which provokes a guarding response instead of range.
Treating it as a strength set, which fatigues the hamstrings before the real work.
benefits: Moves the hamstrings through range under active control instead of a static hold.
Rehearses the hip hinge pattern before loaded deadlift or RDL work.
Needs no equipment and only a few meters of floor space.

name: Rowing Intervals
summary: Repeated hard efforts on the rowing machine separated by easy paddling, with stroke sequence held under fatigue.
instructions: Strap your feet in and set the damper to a moderate setting so the stroke stays quick rather than heavy.
Row easy for a few minutes, then settle at the catch with shins vertical, arms straight and shoulders ahead of the hips.
Start the work bout by driving the legs down hard while the arms stay straight until the legs are almost flat.
Swing the back open from the hips and pull the handle in to the bottom of the ribs to finish the stroke.
Send the hands away first, hinge the body forward, then let the knees bend and slide back to the catch.
Hold that sequence for the full work bout, then drop to light paddling for the recovery and repeat.
mistakes: Opening the back at the same time as the legs, which strains the lower back and leaks power out of the drive.
Rushing the recovery to match the drive, which shortens the next stroke and burns you out before the bout ends.
Chasing stroke rate instead of split, so the rate climbs while the pace on the monitor gets slower.
Sitting still through the rest, which slows waste clearance and leaves the legs heavy for the next effort.
benefits: Trains anaerobic work capacity at a power output continuous rowing never reaches.
Loads upper and lower body in the same interval, which running and cycling intervals do not.
Stays non-impact, so repeated hard efforts cost the joints far less than sprint running.

name: Rowing Sprint
summary: An all-out short rowing effort where stroke rate and leg drive peak together and technique has to survive it.
instructions: Strap in, set a moderate to firm damper, and row easy for several minutes before any hard effort.
Sit at the catch with shins vertical, arms straight and the torso hinged forward from the hips.
Drive the legs down as hard as you can while keeping the arms straight and the back angle fixed.
Snap the back open and pull the handle to the ribs, finishing the stroke with the legs already flat.
Push the hands away fast, rock the torso over, and let the knees rise into the next catch without collapsing.
Hold maximum effort for the planned distance or time, then paddle very light until breathing settles.
mistakes: Letting the recovery speed match the drive, which shortens the stroke and drops pace while the rate climbs.
Yanking with the arms before the legs finish, which cuts the strongest part of the drive out of the stroke.
Pushing the legs and opening the back at the same moment, which is inefficient and loads the lower back.
Judging the effort by stroke rate on the monitor rather than split, so the numbers rise but the pace slows.
benefits: Develops peak power output on a non-impact machine that measures every stroke.
Stresses the anaerobic system hard in efforts short enough to fit any session.
Reveals technique breakdown quickly, which makes it useful as a coaching diagnostic.

name: Running Cooldown
summary: An easy jog after hard running, held at a conversational effort to bring heart rate and breathing back down.
